articles.title: WFTU for Oct. 30 dockworkers’ antiwar action: No sacrifice for imperialist profits & wars!
articles.author: Boston DSA
articles.content: [[{“value”:” The steelworks and docks (Working Mass) This appeal was issued by the World Federation of Trade Unions. The World Federation of Trade Unions issues a militant, class-oriented and internationalist call to its member organizations and trade unions around the world to make the 2nd International Day of Action of Dockworkers on Oct. 30, 2026, their own cause and support it. The mobilization is taking place at a critical time, as military conflicts are spreading and war fronts are dangerously expanding and becoming interconnected, from Ukraine to the Middle East. The murderous state of Israel, with the support of the U.S., the European Union and NATO, continues its crime against the Palestinian people and escalates its military aggression against Iran and Lebanon, increasing the danger of an even broader conflict. Behind the various pretexts lies the conflict among powerful capitalist states and the confrontation between the Euro-Atlantic bloc of the U.S. – NATO – EU and other imperialist centres over markets, energy, raw materials, trade routes and control of strategic infrastructure. Imperialist wars are not a departure from the “normal” functioning of the capitalist system. They are the continuation of exploitation and competition by other means. Billions are being spent on armaments and the war economy, while wages are squeezed, social spending is cut, healthcare and education are commodified and exploitation reaches extreme levels, with exhausting schedules, including 13-hour working days and work seven days a week. The peoples have nothing to gain from wars and the antagonisms of the imperialists. They are called upon to pay for profits, wars and the consequences of a new capitalist economic crisis, to sacrifice themselves for interests that are alien to their own, while business groups claim ever larger shares of the spoils. Ports, railways, airports and transport infrastructure as a whole are being turned into critical hubs for the movement of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops. Workers are being pressured to become cogs in the war machine and accomplices in crimes against the peoples. Dockworkers have already proved that, through organization, collective struggle and coordinated internationalist action, they can prevent ports from being turned into staging grounds for war. They can block the cargoes of death that fuel the Israeli state’s slaughter of the Palestinian people and the spread of war throughout the Middle East. February 2026 action in 20 ports On Feb 6, 2026, strike action was held in 20 ports across seven countries. In May, in Istanbul, trade union organizations from 35 ports formed a coordination network, which now encompasses more than 40 ports across the Mediterranean and Europe, with the participation of organizations from France, Greece, the Basque Country, Türkiye, Morocco and Italy, under the slogan: “Dockworkers do not work for war.” On Oct. 30, trade unions will hold new militant actions and strikes. The common framework “Ports for Peace – Jobs with Dignity” links the struggle against imperialist war with the fight for Collective Labor Agreements, wage increases, stable employment, shorter working hours and substantive health and safety measures. This is also linked to opposition to privatizations, subcontracted and temporary employment and the use of automation and artificial intelligence to eliminate jobs and intensify exploitation. Technological and scientific progress must serve to reduce working time and improve workers’ lives, not the profitability of the monopolies. The experience of dockworkers has wider significance for workers in the metal industry and shipyards, railways, energy, telecommunications, transport and logistics. These sectors connect ports, industrial zones and military infrastructure and can play a decisive role in the common struggle against imperialist war and exploitation. October 30 can mark a major new step in the international, militant coordination of the working class. From port to port, in every workplace and sector, from country to country, workers are sending the message that they will not choose between the camps of their exploiters, will not become cogs in their war machine and will not sacrifice their lives and rights for the profits of the monopolies. No sacrifice for the profits and wars of the imperialists! Long live the internationalist solidarity of the working class! The World Federation of Trade Unions (WFTU) is an international federation of trade unions established on October 3, 1945. Founded in the immediate aftermath of World War II, the organization built on the pre-war legacy of the International Federation of Trade Unions as a single structure for trade unions world-wide, following the World Trade Union Conference in London, United Kingdom. The federation went from representing 48 million workers in 2005 to 105 million in 2022. articles.title: Representation Is Not Liberation
articles.author: Melina Abdullah
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. “You’re not supporting Karen for mayor?!?!? Wow. That’s crazy!” Before I could make it in the door to the voter education event, a longtime sister-friend greeted me with those words of hello. Not a hug or a “thanks for coming.” My response? “I think it’s crazy to give away a billion dollars in raises to police, to appoint Jim McDonnell as chief, and to call it not-a-genocide in Palestine.” Days before the election, it is not my intent to write another column critical of the current mayor. I have tried to lovingly call her in with previous pieces in hopes of her changing course. That did not happen and I will vote accordingly. But this piece is not about Karen Bass. It is about reminding ourselves why we vote. At a time when access, being at tables and in rooms, is peddled as a reason to vote for candidates, we must remember that we are voting for policymakers, not prom queens. Our votes are not about who we like best or even who looks like us, but who is most aligned with or can be pushed to enact policies that advance our collective agendas, values, and vision. In many ways, election season is a time for self-reflection. We must ask ourselves what we actually believe in. What are our moral minimums? Many have asked me to produce a voter guide. There are some strong guides already in circulation. (I especially appreciate those published by the Black Los Angeles Young Democrats and Black Women for Wellness.) Rather than writing my own, I posted my moral minimums. Here is what I came up with. Related: The Black Panthers at 60: Black Liberation Was Never Just About Voting Black Lives Matter: Prioritize the liberation of Black people. When Black people get free, everybody gets free. F the Pol(ICE): Police descend from slavecatching, prisons from plantations, and ICE is a part of the larger infrastructure. There is no redeeming any of them. Point blank period. We want a strong robust community-based public safety system. Candidates who take money and endorsements from police associations are pledging their allegiance to them, and turning their backs on the people. Reparations Now: Reparations is a basic human right and core international legal principle. Black reparations must be paid to Black people for chattel slavery, the de facto slavery and segregation that followed, and every tentacle of Black oppression and dehumanization that remains and has yet to be dismantled. Free Palestine: Palestinians have a right to life and self-determination. Those who take money from the Israeli lobby condone genocide. They have no place. Free Palestine. Free Congo. Free Sudan. People over profits: Life and well-being are sacred. There is no thing or luxury more important than life. We have the collective right to good lives and to ownership over our own selves and beings. Workers’ rights over corporate greed. Liberated Ethnic Studies: We want an educational system that teaches our children the truth and empowers them as critical thinkers and informed actors. This means well-funded ethnic studies curricula and intentional, directed, school programs that provide critical supports. Free the land: Protect the planet. Support land-back to restore Indigenous stewardship. Advance Black autonomy. Related: Remembering Curtis Renee: Seven Lessons in Love, Liberation, and Revolution Solidarity forever: Stand in solidarity with Black people, Indigenous communities, LGBTQIA+ folks, women, workers, people with disabilities, the poor, and all oppressed people at home and around the world. I spent a few weeks reflecting to develop these. After posting on social media, others also weighed in. “What about environmental justice? Bodily autonomy? Ending sexual violence? What about stopping surveillance and the rise of the ‘stalker state?’ What do we do about Donald Trump and his legion of demons?” To be clear, this is by no means a complete list. There are glaring omissions here. But it is a start. Establishing and affirming my own moral minimums helps me not be duped by the tall Black man in the suit with a compelling life story running for City Attorney, who promises to prosecute protestors “only if they break the law.” Instead, moral minimums bring me to research who’s paying for John McKinney’s campaign and uncover millions in independent expenditures by cops, corporations, and MAGA groups. With just days to go before the ballot deadline. May we all reflect on our own moral minimums and use them to guide our vote. And then, the day after election day, let’s use them to guide our organizing and the necessary action to hold electeds accountable and do the real work of building the world that we all want, need, and deserve. The Los Angeles Sentinel

articles.title: Why LA Progressive Is Changing Its Voter Guide Recommendation to Colin Hernandez
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. LA Progressive has updated its Progressive Voter Guide for California’s 51st Assembly District, replacing Rick Chavez Zbur with Colin Hernandez. A reader recently asked us to revisit this race, pointing to a contradiction between our publication’s defense of free expression and Zbur’s role as a lead author of Assembly Bill 715. That request deserved a serious response. Our voter guide is intended to help readers make informed choices. When readers raise substantive concerns about its contents, we have a responsibility to examine them—and to make changes when the evidence warrants it. Readers ultimately decide which candidates best represent their values and priorities. AB 715, signed into law in October 2025, was presented as a measure to combat antisemitism and discrimination in California schools. Protecting Jewish students from harassment and discrimination is essential. The question is whether the law’s approach adequately protects freedom of expression alongside that obligation. ACLU California Action opposed AB 715, warning that it could chill constitutionally protected classroom discussion and undermine academic freedom. These concerns deserve particular attention when teachers discuss Israel, Palestine, and human rights—subjects on which political criticism must not automatically be treated as discrimination. The law permits members of the public, including anonymous complainants, to file complaints alleging that instructional materials violate its antidiscrimination requirements, provided they supply evidence or information leading to evidence. That does not mean mentioning Gaza is itself prohibited. Our concern is that a broad complaint process can encourage educators to avoid difficult subjects rather than risk an investigation. In an article published by LA Progressive, civil liberties attorney Stephen Rohde examined the First Amendment concerns surrounding AB 715 and the danger of conflating criticism of Israel with antisemitism. His analysis underscores a principle central to our coverage: protecting students from discrimination and protecting political expression are obligations that must be upheld together. Hernandez’s published platform explicitly opposes AB 715 and calls for protecting teachers’ academic freedom. He also supports universal healthcare through CalCare, expanded social housing, stronger tenant protections, universal childcare, and greater contributions from billionaires and large corporations. His immigration platform calls for abolishing ICE and expanding access to legal representation for people facing deportation. These positions explain his inclusion in the updated guide. They reflect an approach that treats housing, healthcare, education, and human dignity as public responsibilities and provide readers with substantive differences to consider in this race. Our voter guide should reflect careful examination of the candidates and the issues. That requires a willingness to listen, revisit earlier judgments, and explain changes openly. We thank the reader who brought these concerns to our attention. The updated entry for California’s 51st Assembly District now lists Colin Hernandez.

articles.title: Coalition to Protest Lynn Fitch’s Decision in Police Killing of Baby Kohen Wiley
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Press Release Black Lives Matter Grassroots, Building Bridges Coalition, Movement for Black Lives, Jackson People’s Assembly, and a host of community groups are planning to protest Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch to unequivocally denounce her determination that the murder of baby Kohen Wiley was “justified.” Senatobia police Sergeant Hunter Foster. Foster, who has a documented history of racism and violence, shot the one-year-old dead in his mother’s arms on June 14, 2026. This is one of the most egregious and horrifying acts of anti-Black violence that we have seen from police anywhere. Police should have never been called. Sergeant Foster should never have fired his weapon. And the murder can never be justified. We have had enough of white supremacist systems terrorizing our communities and stealing Black lives, with no liability or consequence.. Foster resigned from the Senatobia police department last week in light of leaked video footage that shows him shooting into the passenger side of the vehicle where Baby Kohen was being held by his mother. Murderous cop Hunter Foster shot into the car - striking the friend and killing Baby Kohen. Foster was clearly out of the path of the vehicle that he pursued on foot. Neither the mother or her friend were suspected of any crime. “What kind of world is this when the murder of a baby could ever be deemed ‘justified’? Senatobia police, Lynn Fitch, and Walmart all have blood on their hands and there must be consequences. They don’t get to murder our babies with impunity,” says Dr. Melina Abdullah of Black Lives Matter Grassroots. We condemn Walmart for calling police on a Black mother. We condemn killer cop Hunter Foster for shooting a precious Black baby. We condemn the Senatobia Police Department for serving as a breeding ground for racist violence and greenlighting the killing and terrorization of Black people. We condemn Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch for giving the green light to police to kill - even babies - with absolute impunity. Memorials for Baby Kohen have already restarted. November 1st marks what should have been Baby Kohen’s second birthday. Black Lives Matter Grassroots and Building Bridges Coalition are planning a weekend of events in collaboration with Baby Kohen’s family in both Senatobia and Jackson, Mississippi. These activations are meant to memorialize his short life, support community healing and empowerment, and rally for justice in Kohen’s name. “Kohen’s entire family is in unimaginable pain. They should be celebrating his birthday, not mourning his death. The community is organizing and demanding accountability,” says Marquell Bridges, of the Building Bridges Coalition, who has been organizing alongside Kohen’s family since the killing. In addition, from October 30th through November 2nd, Baby Kohen’s family, Black Lives Matter Grassroots and the Building Bridges Coalition is calling for community to: Boycott Walmart. Demand the firing of killer cop Hunter Foster. Oppose Attorney General Lynn Fitch, especially in her bid for Mississippi Governor. Pluginwith @blmgrassroots on Instagram for next steps. Justice in the name of Baby Kohen Wiley! articles.title: Caring for Children
articles.author: Colin Greer, Reynard Loki
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Children form their understanding of society through the people around them: the person who greets them at the classroom door, the coach who notices when something’s wrong, the nurse who explains a scary procedure gently, the librarian who saves a book, the neighbor who walks them home. Policy, institutions, and cultural norms—the subjects of the first five articles in this series—often reach children through these adults. A well-funded program or a well-written law can change a child’s circumstances. But children often experience its promise through something much simpler: a lunch, a lesson, a kind word, a moment of attention. Researchers at Harvard University’s Center on the Developing Child describe “ serve and return ” as the responsive, back-and-forth exchanges between children and the adults who care for them. Because these relationships help shape the developing brain, the adults present in a child’s early years play a foundational role. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) framework on “Preventing Adverse Childhood Experiences” identifies safe, stable, nurturing relationships as critical not only to helping children reach their full potential but also to preventing harm. Trusted adults help child-welfare policy fulfill its promise. And yet many of these adults—teachers, coaches, childcare workers, librarians, volunteers, and others—work with limited time, resources, autonomy, or institutional support. If society relies on these relationships to protect children and support their development, it has an obligation to strengthen the people who sustain them. That raises a central question: How can society better recognize, support, and organize the adults who already care for children—and expand what they can offer? Related: A Public-Private Model for Youth Opportunity: Investing in Care The Adults Children Actually Encounter Every Day A child’s daily life brings them into contact with a wide range of adults: their third-grade teacher, youth soccer coach, pediatrician, neighborhood librarian, daycare provider, music teacher, crossing guard, or scout leader. The volunteer who runs the after-school program and the neighbor who keeps an eye on the block also matter. Together, these adults form part of the child’s social world. These adults have different roles and responsibilities, but children do not necessarily see them through their professional roles. A teacher may notice that a child has arrived hungry. A coach may recognize that something is wrong before the child says so. A librarian may become someone a child trusts enough to approach for help. Their importance can extend well beyond the task they were hired or volunteered to perform. One finding recurs in research on childhood resilience: relationships with supportive adults matter. Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child identifies at least one stable, committed relationship with a supportive parent, caregiver, or other adult as a common protective factor for children who overcome serious hardship. Trusted relationships with adults outside the immediate family also matter. In a 2021 study , Kathryn Ashton of Public Health Wales and her colleagues examined adults’ recollections of the support available to them during childhood, including from trusted adults outside the home. They found that access to trusted adults was associated with greater childhood resilience resources, particularly among those who had experienced substantial adversity. What matters is not only what these adults do, but whether they know a child well enough to notice a change, recognize a need, or earn their trust. But how much attention an adult can give a child depends in part on how many children that adult is expected to care for. The Privilege of Adult Attention That makes adult-to-child ratios consequential. A teacher responsible for 30 students has far less time for each child than a tutor working one-on-one. A coach responsible for an entire team has less time for each player than an instructor working individually with one child. Smaller adult-to-child ratios give adults more opportunities to notice changes , recognize needs, build trust, and respond. Families with resources can pay for more adult attention. They hire tutors, coaches, therapists, and music teachers. They may choose schools with smaller classes or programs offering more individual attention. What they are buying is more of an adult’s time and attention for fewer children. What affluent families seek for their own children raises a larger question. Why should close adult attention be treated primarily as a private advantage rather than something every child should have? The goal cannot always be one adult for one child, nor will the ratio be the same in a classroom, sports team, childcare center, or after-school program. But the principle can be universal: every child should have meaningful access to adults who have enough time and capacity to know them. That would make adult-to-child ratios more than an administrative staffing measure. Those ratios would also tell us something about how much room a community makes for those relationships. Related: The Hidden Cost of Neglecting Youth Health is a Bill We All Pay Beyond the Job Description The adults who matter to children sometimes become important for reasons that have little to do with the duties for which they were hired. A teacher teaches, a pediatrician provides medical care, a librarian helps people find information, a coach develops athletic skills, and a crossing guard gets children safely across the street. But each may notice something that someone farther from the child would miss. A teacher may notice that a student is hungry or unusually withdrawn. A coach may realize that a child is struggling with a problem at home. A librarian may become an adult a teenager trusts enough to approach for help. A pediatrician may recognize signs that a child is unsafe . A crossing guard who sees the same children every morning may notice when one of them suddenly seems frightened or upset. None of these observations necessarily form part of a job description, but noticing them may still call for a response. Standing up for a child in such circumstances need not be heroic. It can be an ordinary part of caring for children: noticing what they need, speaking up for them, and helping when one can. This does not mean that every adult who works with children should assume responsibilities for which they are unqualified, or that professional boundaries do not matter. It means that a job description cannot anticipate every circumstance in which an adult may be called upon to notice, listen, help, or find someone who can. An extraordinary act of care can make other adults reconsider what their own responsibilities require. Their value is not simply that they give us heroes to admire. A teacher who takes unusual steps to protect a student, for example, may prompt other teachers to consider where their own responsibility begins and ends. The exceptional case enlarges the question. Extraordinary acts can reveal how far the responsibility to care for a child may sometimes extend. What matters every day is readiness: the willingness to recognize a child’s need and respond appropriately, even when the need falls outside the ordinary expectations of one’s role. Related: Criminalizing Childhood: Our Justice System Failing America’s Youth Respecting the People Who Care for Children If we ask adults to be ready to respond to a child’s needs, we owe them support in return. We cannot ask teachers, childcare workers, coaches, librarians, healthcare workers, and others to enlarge their sense of responsibility while the institutions around them withdraw support. People who care for children need adequate compensation, manageable workloads, useful training, professional autonomy, and institutional support when a child needs more help than one person can provide. A teacher with too many students has less time to notice what is happening with each one. A childcare worker worried about making rent is being asked to carry financial strain alongside demanding work. A coach or youth worker who recognizes that a child is in trouble needs to know where to turn next. The people paid to care for children have long been undervalued. Childcare workers, daycare aides, babysitters, and others who care for children have frequently been poorly compensated, reflecting in part the historical devaluation of caregiving traditionally performed by mothers. Taking this work seriously means recognizing it as skilled and consequential work, with compensation and professional development opportunities to match. Head Start , a federally funded program, offers one example. From its beginnings in the 1960s, the program was designed not only to serve children but also to involve parents and create opportunities for training, employment, and professional development . This two-generation approach recognized that strengthening the adults around children could strengthen children’s lives, too. Gratitude is not enough. Respect means recognizing that their judgment, time, and well-being matter. Training can help professionals who work with children recognize signs of trauma , abuse, distress, or other needs, but training alone is not enough. They also need clear pathways to additional help and the confidence that an institution will support appropriate action rather than leave them to manage a difficult situation alone. Teachers make the problem especially visible because they spend so much time with children, but the same needs recur wherever adults are responsible for children. Support gives adults more room to pay attention, build trust, exercise judgment, and respond when they notice a change in a child. Bottom line: caring for children includes caring for the people responsible for them. Related: The Hidden Crisis: How America Fails to Protect Its Children Communities That Empower Caregivers Communities can ask what would help caregivers respond when a child needs something beyond the ordinary boundaries of their role. Sometimes the answer is modest: a small amount of discretionary money, enough time for a conversation, the authority to make a reasonable decision, or a direct connection to someone who can help. Flexible funds offer one model. A trusted adult who knows a child needs glasses, transportation, food, clothing, or another immediate necessity may be better positioned to recognize the urgency than a distant administrator. The principle is simple: place modest, discretionary resources closer to the people who can see where they are needed. As we have seen, no caregiver can meet every need. A teacher may recognize a health problem but need a nurse or physician to diagnose and treat it. A coach may learn about trouble at home but needs a social worker or another appropriate professional. Communities can make these connections easier by building relationships among the adults and organizations that serve the same children. Those connections would help caregivers share knowledge, coordinate services, and tackle problems beyond any one person’s reach. Professional boundaries still matter. The aim is to make it easier for someone who notices a problem to reach someone equipped to address it. Schools, libraries, and other institutions that serve children could also host local discussions about what children need. Caregivers, families, residents, and experts could hear one another, consider the evidence, and help decide what would best serve children in their community. Money is not the only resource a community can organize. Time dollars and related time-banking models use time as the unit of exchange: an hour of service earns a time credit that can be used for another service. Applied to the institutions and networks surrounding children, such exchanges could allow volunteers, caregivers, and other community members to contribute what they know how to do and receive help in return. The same attention to children can shape decisions at the city level. The Van Leer Foundation’s Urban95 initiative asks planners and policymakers to consider a city “from an elevation of 95 centimeters”—the approximate height of a 3-year-old. That shift in perspective has informed work on public space, transportation, neighborhood services, and other features of urban life that affect young children and their caregivers. There may also be value in creating local and national organizations that bring together people whose work brings them into children’s lives. Teachers, childcare workers, healthcare professionals, coaches, librarians, mentors, and others already have professional associations, unions, and other places to exchange knowledge within their fields. Less common are opportunities for them to talk across those boundaries about the children they collectively serve. Interprofessional organizations could create those connections, helping caregivers share knowledge, advocate for the conditions children need, and support one another. These connections can also help communities recognize when families need support. Supporting parents and other caregivers in meeting basic needs is another way of supporting children. Local communities, however, do not always have the resources to meet these needs on their own. Care for children therefore also depends on public programs beyond the local level. Nutrition assistance, healthcare coverage, hospitals, and other state and national systems require public support to remain reliable and accessible. People who care about children can become advocates for those systems—paying attention to whether public policy strengthens or weakens the supports children and families depend on, and carrying that knowledge into civic life and the voting booth. Communities already organize people to be ready when others need help. Volunteer fire departments offer one familiar example: people with different occupations maintain relationships, training, and a shared readiness to respond. Networks among people who care for children could serve a related purpose—not by turning every caregiver into a specialist, but by making it easier to find the right person or resource when an ordinary need or an emergency arises. When someone notices that a child needs help, the community’s response should not end with that observation. Sometimes caring means helping directly; sometimes it means knowing who else can. The adult should have somewhere to turn, something to draw upon, and enough freedom to act. If we care about children, we also need to care for the people who care for them. But the circle of responsibility does not end with those who work with children every day. In the end, we are all caregivers of children because the communities we build, the institutions we support, and the public choices we make help determine the conditions in which children grow. Caring for children therefore means more than helping when a child is directly within our reach. Standing up for them is everyone’s responsibility. articles.title: National Security Has Failed
articles.author: Lawrence S. Wittner
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For millennia, the world’s people have been kidding themselves about national security. Worried about the survival of their nation in a world of self-interested, sometimes aggressive nations, people have armed and prepared themselves for war. Only military strength, they have assumed, would fend off or defeat a military attack on their nation. And a case can be made for this assumption, for not all nations–and not all people–are willing to deal peacefully or justly with their neighbors. Even so, over the course of human history, this reliance upon national military might to defend national security has produced disaster after disaster. Although almost every country has armed itself for national defense, even those with immense military might have ended up fighting recurring wars to defend what they regard as their national security. Just look at the history of the “great powers” of recent centuries–the United States, Russia, China, Britain, France, Germany, and Japan–and consider how frequently they have waged war, sometimes emerging as the victors and other times as the vanquished. Related: Trump's War on the International Criminal Court Threatens Global Justice Furthermore, preparing for and fighting wars, even victorious wars, have come at an immense human cost. Estimates for the death toll in the almost constant flow of wars over the span of human history range as high as 1 billion people . And to this we should add the vast numbers of people crippled, blinded, traumatized, and left homeless. Russia’s current military invasion of Ukraine, aside from slaughtering large numbers of Ukrainians, has already led to the deaths or injuries of 1,581,840 Russian soldiers . Nuclear war , of course, promises to increase war’s human toll very substantially, with the living, as is sometimes said, envying the dead. Nevertheless, the nations of the world continue, relentlessly, to arm and prepare themselves for war. Global military expenditures rose by nearly three percent in 2025, the 11 th consecutive year of growth, reaching $2.9 trillion. America’s Donald Trump, a fervent supporter of U.S. military power, has proposed a 42 percent increase in the forthcoming U.S. military budget to $1.5 trillion about 63 percent of federal discretionary spending. Of course, far-sighted individuals have criticized militarism and war, as well as suggested better ways for nations to relate to one another. Thanks particularly to the massive slaughter and destruction wrought by the two World Wars, they called for the development of international institutions that could safeguard national security through the development and enforcement of international law. This agitation led to the establishment of the League of Nations (and its legal arm, the Permanent Court of International Justice) and, near the end of World War II, to the establishment of the League’s successor, the United Nations (and its legal arm, the International Court of Justice). Related: How Trump’s Labor Policies Are Cutting Worker Pay These new institutions were met with considerable enthusiasm by a war-weary public, and even by many national officials, who recognized that, if every country continued blindly pursuing what it viewed as its own interests, global conflict and war were inevitable. But this potential turning point in human history was bedeviled by two major problems. For thousands of years, nations had defended their “interests” (and especially their national security) through military might. Consequently, many government officials and even many members of the public were not accustomed to thinking and behaving according to what best served the common good. Furthermore, the great powers were particularly reluctant to surrender the advantages, including empire, that military might traditionally afforded them in world affairs. As a result, the leaders of the major powers, despite their rhetoric about the equality of nations and collective action to cope with international issues, remained committed to ensuring a privileged status for their own countries. In the case of the League of Nations, this reluctance to accept limits meant that the great power victors in World War I came away from the peace settlement with new territory, including the spoils of empire (disguised as “mandates”), taken from the war’s great power losers. Moreover, in subsequent years, the Axis nations plunged into war to restore their empires or enhance them, while they and other major powers withdrew from the League when it condemned their belligerent behavior. The U.S. government never even joined the League. Related: Trump’s Canada Crisis Shows How Fragile Alliances Really Are When it came to the United Nations, the great power victors in World War II established a UN Security Council that provided each of them with a veto over collective action for international security. Thus, they could (and did) veto such action when they felt it adversely affected them or their friends. They also pursued what they regarded as their national security by subverting, invading, and even occupying other nations, while occasionally withholding their dues payments to the world organization. Against this backdrop, it’s easy to conclude that international security has failed the test. But, given the existence of key international institutions for only a tiny portion of human history, isn’t it premature to abandon efforts to create an effective international security system? After all, the United Nations is only 81 years old. By contrast, modern human beings have been around for about 300,000 years . Also, what is the alternative? Surely it is endless war, capped off by the use of nuclear weapons to annihilate the human race. So, in our current predicament, let’s give some thought to strengthening the world’s international institutions. Numerous nations have called for reforming the United Nations. Modest measures, such as providing it with adequate funding and enhancing the role of the General Assembly, can be fairly easily implemented. More significant changes–for example, abolishing the Security Council veto–will take a more substantial effort, including the holding of a UN Charter review conference . Article 109 of the UN Charter provides the framework for such a conference, and an Article 109 Coalition has recently launched a campaign to prepare for it. Over thousands of years, war and militarism have failed to safeguard national security. But international security might finally succeed at the task. PeaceVoice

articles.title: Only Israel’s Palestinians Vote Against Genocide
articles.author: Matan Kaminer
articles.content: It was heralded by many as “the most consequential election in Israeli history,” and by rights it should have been. Under Benjamin Netanyahu’s outgoing far-right government, Israel plunged into a severe constitutional crisis, suffered the worst military setback in its history, carried out a genocide in Gaza and two failed wars in Iran, and become the most hated country in the world. And yet, as Haaretz editor Aluf Benn noted in his postmortem , Israeli Jewish voters proved themselves imperturbable. Support for aggression throughout the region remains nearly universal among Jewish voters, who have once again sorted themselves again into pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs on a basis that, while reflecting real class divisions , is expressed in familiar culture-war terms, producing yet another frustrating stalemate. There is, however, one dramatic exception to this uncanny stasis: Israel’s Palestinian minority, which responded to unprecedented levels of racist incitement with the highest turnout on record. Of over eight hundred thousand votes cast by Palestinian citizens, 37 percent went to the Islamist United Arab List (UAL, also known as Ra’am), and 51 percent to the Joint List, which unites communists, left-liberals and independents. As a result, nineteen out of 120 seats in the Knesset, which are allocated proportionally, have gone to Israel’s only two non-Zionist parties, each of which also has one Jewish representative. (Support for these parties among Jews is numerically insignificant, though hundreds of Jewish academics signed a petition in support of the Joint List.) In stark contrast to the violence and malaise that have gripped Israel’s Palestinian community following the rise of state-tolerated organized crime , the contest between the two parties was peaceful and restrained. This is all the more remarkable given the clear ideological divide between them. The Joint List couples the demand for civic equality for Palestinian citizens with a clear rejection of Israel’s annihilationist policy in Gaza and its ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Meanwhile, the UAL — a prominent member of the original Joint List — has turned to a sectoral strategy modeled on that of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Following his 2021 split from the Joint List, UAL leader Mansour Abbas courted Netanyahu and then served as a junior partner in the government that briefly ousted him in 2021–22. This time around, the anti-Netanyahu bloc has drawn the bar for cooperation at a level meant to exclude even the UAL. Its leader du jour, Lieutenant General Gadi Eisenkot, clarified that any party seeking to join him in government would have to declare Hamas — which still is hanging onto power in Gaza — a “terrorist organization which must be annihilated.” As Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, Eisenkot elaborated the infamous “Dahiya doctrine,” which recommends mass killing of civilians in areas dominated by hostile forces. In the current context, his shibboleth cannot be read as anything but a demand for active consent to ongoing genocide. The hostility of the Zionist opposition to any form of solidarity with Gaza was driven home when all its parties, including the liberal Democrats , backed an election board decision to bar Joint List candidate Sami Abu-Shehadeh from running on the basis of a vaguely celebratory article written on October 7 and subsequently repudiated. (Genocidal expressions by right-wing candidates, it goes without saying, were not censured in the same way.) Against Abstention Given the depth of the racist rejectionism Palestinian citizens have suffered from both Zionist blocs and the eager complicity of both in colonial violence, a turn to abstention would not be unexpected. But Israel’s Palestinian citizens do not have the luxury of ignoring the differences between these blocs, small as they may be. Thus, Netanyahu’s finance minister and West Bank Viceroy Bezalel Smotrich has empowered settler militias to carry out a campaign of ethnic cleansing that might be halted, if not reversed, under an Eisenkot administration. His ghoulish national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has made a fetish out of torturing and executing Palestinian prisoners. High Palestinian turnout has severely weakened extreme-right parties led by the two and prevented two others from crossing the representation threshold, depriving Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority. Voters are justified in hoping a new government will dial back its ferocity on both fronts as well as tackling organized crime more seriously. For Palestinians, these are questions of life and death, if not of imminent decolonization. Under these complex circumstances, voters have rewarded the Joint List for striking a balance between principle and pragmatism. Sociologist Maha Sabbah-Karkabi, who will be joining the Knesset as a Joint List representative, stressed the importance of Palestinians’ show of collective power. “By fully utilizing their electoral potential,” she told me, they “have repositioned themselves at the center of Israel’s political landscape.” However, Sabbah-Karkabi added, the Joint List now confronts a “climate of delegitimization of Arab political participation coming from different parts of the political spectrum,” rendering the question of influencing government policy “much more complicated.” Delegitimization has come swiftly from Netanyahu’s propaganda organs, which quickly coined the felicitous oxymoron “ ballot box terrorism ” while weakly claiming Qatari interference on the Joint List’s behalf. (Netanyahu’s advisers, of course, are the ones who have worked for Qatar.) But while Eisenkot and most of his allies obstinately continue to refuse any alliance with Palestinian parties, the Democrats are finally beginning to peel away from this boneheaded consensus. For the Joint List, the situation presents opportunities as well as risks. Sabbah-Karkabi and Amjad Shbita, general secretary of the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality (the largest of the Joint List’s components), agree that seeing Netanyahu and his far-right government replaced is an urgent priority. Unlike the UAL’s deputies, however, they are also committed to Palestinian national solidarity across borders. The electorate has endorsed this commitment in no uncertain terms. The ball is now in the court of Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc. To avoid a return election, he will have to break one of two campaign promises: not to enter a coalition with Netanyahu, and to avoid relying on “Arab votes.” If he reneges on the former vow — perhaps under cover of a new war with Iran, conveniently started by Donald Trump and Netanyahu in the coming weeks — he will gift the latter with a renewed sheen of invincibility and the international legitimacy he has done so much to lose. To end Netanyahu’s rule, Eisenkot would have to break the racist taboo on negotiation with the Palestinian public’s representatives. Though it will not join an Eisenkot government, Shbita told me, the Joint List would be willing to provide it with a parliamentary safety net, preventing Netanyahu from getting another shot at power by bringing the government down with a vote of no confidence. Even if Eisenkot lacks the courage to negotiate such an agreement, Shbita added, “we would consider enabling a minority government by not voting it down “until Netanyahu’s departure from the political scene becomes a certainty.” Following the “most consequential election in its history,” the political scene in Israel continues to look unbearably bleak. Progressives elsewhere have no reason to let up the pressure for broad sanctions and a total arms embargo. Nevertheless, they can take inspiration from the many Palestinian (and a few Jewish) citizens of Israel, who by voting for the Joint List have expressed their steadfastness — sumoud — in the struggle for democracy, justice, and peace. articles.title: Impressions (October 2026)
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: Impressions is where ROC DSA members can share what they’re reading, listening to, viewing, or otherwise experiencing. If you have two hundred words about the culture at large you’d like to share with your comrades, submit to Rich J on Slack or to the Red Star at steering@rocdsa.org . Trans, Punk, and Somehow Legal? Abigail J watched: The People’s Joker I recently stumbled upon what is easily one of my new top 5 movies, The People’s Joker by Vera Drew (2022). This movie is an insane transgender coming of age story set in an unofficial DC Comics universe and presented in a psychedelic mixed media format (complete with live action, stop motion, and 2-D animation). The production and editing were completely crowd-sourced, and I’m genuinely not sure how this legally got made. As a (very recently out) trans woman, this movie hit me in a way that almost no other movie or show has before. During production, this movie morphed from simply being a compilation of Batman satires to a semi-autobiographical narrative of Vera Drew’s life and transition up to that point (the creator and main star). While my story has definitely been different than both Vera’s and the ritual People’s Joker’s, I finally saw aspects of my life represented on film that I had never seen before, and connected to on a visceral level. How would my life be different if I’d seen this five, ten, fifteen years ago? I’ll never know, but I hope some not-yet-aware trans teens get as much (or more) out of this movie than I did. For those interested, the film is available for free at: www.thepeoplesjoker.com Real Americans Isabella D watched: The Americans Elizabeth and Philip Jennings are the quintessential family in Reagan’s America — two kids, a nice house in the suburbs, respectable careers. Their neighbors, and certainly not the affable FBI agent across the street, would never suspect that the two are KGB spies, committing gruesome acts of espionage to tip the scales of the Cold War in the Soviet Union’s favor. Over the course of six seasons, audiences suffer Breaking Bad-esque tension over if and when the Jennings will be found out in The Americans . I mostly enjoyed the series, but with a disclaimer: while the show is a well-crafted drama with four Emmys under its belt, the acute viewer may discern the tint of anti-Communist, pro-western ideals. This gripe is not just paranoia; the creator and showrunner Joe Weisberg is a Reagan-admiring former CIA agent. The Jennings are depicted as destroying themselves for a vague cause, their Marxist convictions never fully elucidated, and dogmatically resisting the prosperous American way of life for an oppressive, decadent Soviet Union. The cinematographic dichotomy alone relays this bias — the US is colorful, vibrant, abundant, and the USSR bleak, dismal, and bureaucratically stifling. To give credit where credit is due, the narrative imparts a great deal of empathy and relatability to Elizabeth and Philip as Soviet illegals before a predominantly western audience. The couple’s dynamic is deeply compelling, tempering my ideological frustration with the show, but the narrative is dragged down by clunky plotlines and a clear predilection for the American way. Rooting for the Underdog. Greg LH watched: Coyote vs. ACME In Coyote vs. ACME , our ever-floundering Wile E. Coyote, and his billboard lawyer Kevin Avery (Will Forte), become the face of underdogs confronting the corporate behemoth ACME over the thousands of malfunctioning products sold to the Coyote. Coyote vs. ACME has a convoluted production history – In 2023 Warner Bros. shelved the fully-made film to obtain a $30 million tax write-off. The film was only released in 2026 following backlash and its subsequent purchase by another production company. On opening day at The Little Theater, Dan Sendker, author of Dance of the Comedians – 75 Years of the Road Runner and Wile E. Coyote gave this context prior to the showing, echoing the content of the film and highlighting the perverted incentives of capitalism. The film delivers the laughs and delights of the original cartoon, with the fun element of live-action overlap. A tale of the little guy going after the corporate behemoth, the Coyote manages to poke his snout at corporate malfeasance. But his revenge is individualistic – there is no moment of organized unity with the other injured members of his class (of cartoon characters). I was hoping for a class action lawsuit, at least. A montage of FBI arrests also places the ideology of the movie within the Mueller-led resistance of Trump One. Don’t think about it too deeply though, just go have a good time. articles.title: UAW Members’ Demands Will Shape Next Congress as Union Runs its Most Ambitious Electoral Program in Decades
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: After months of organizing that began early in the summer, the UAW is on track to knock more than 300,000 doors with UAW members and union households as part of its biggest electoral program in decades. The UAW is using its membership-focused political program, modeled on the success of the 2023 Stand Up Strike, to reach working-class voters from UAW households in key Senate and House races nationwide. In several key districts where UAW membership exceeds the previous election’s margin of victory, the UAW has more than 130 full-time political organizers in the field and has mobilized thousands of volunteers. The focus of the program has been empowering members to have honest conversations with UAW families about UAW’s core four issues: wages, healthcare, retirement, and time off. Since launching in July, the member-led program has reached hundreds of thousands of working-class voters across Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, California, Nevada, Alaska, Arizona, Washington, North Carolina, Kansas, Texas, Pennsylvania, New York and Maine. The groundwork has been substantial. By election day, the union projects it will have completed: More than 300,000 doors knocked 750,000 calls made More than 4,000 volunteers recruited “Our political program is like everything else about the UAW: it’s member-driven,” said UAW President Shawn Fain. “We’ve been flexing our muscle at the bargaining table for the last few years. Now we’re building that same muscle in our politics. This year, our members are leading a bold political program, shaking up the political status quo. We’ll start by electing UAW champions to office – but our members will lead the work that comes after election day to win a working-class agenda in the halls of power.” Organizing Where Members Can Make the Difference Michigan and Ohio are central to the effort, reflecting the importance of industrial jobs, economic security, and workers’ rights in the region’s political landscape. “I have been knocking doors in elections for 25 years, and this one has had more energy than I’ve felt in a long time talking to UAW voters and their families,” said Tielece Perry, UAW Local 7 member from Belleville, MI. “Talking about being able to make ends meet is what we do with our coworkers every time we are bargaining a new union contract, and affordability is by far the number one issue voters care about right now. The UAW has the organizational structure, the relationships across Michigan, and the vision to turn those concerns into collective action — and real votes for our endorsed slate.” In Ohio, the UAW has committed significant resources to bring Sherrod Brown, a longtime ally of working-class people, back to the Senate. The Union is also working to protect Marcy Kaptur’s seat in District 09, one of the country’s densest UAW districts, where members make up 10% of all voters. Members are also working to flip District 07 for fellow union member Brian Poindexter. In Lorain County—the only Ohio county to vote for both Sherrod Brown and Donald Trump in 2024—the UAW has added a contentious County Commission race to its campaign. UAW-represented county workers have been on strike since February 18, underscoring the connection between political decisions and workers’ ability to secure fair treatment on the job. “I’ve been active in CAP for a long time now and this year is different from previous years,” said Kim Daniels, a UAW Local 12 member in Toledo, OH. “For months, our boots have been on the ground throughout the state of Ohio. With our unity and power, Ohio will become the number one state for working-class people. This program will be the driving force for Ohio.” “I’m really proud to be involved with the UAW’s political program this election cycle,” said Shawn Smith, a UAW Local 677 member in Allentown, PA. “I’ve noticed there’s less negativity towards us at doors, no matter which side someone is on. We all realize we are going in the wrong direction where nothing is affordable anymore. Our UAW program isn’t just about UAW members – it’s about fighting to lift up the entire working-class with candidates like our union brother Bob Brooks in PA-07.” “Serving on UAW’s release staff this fall has changed my life. For the first time, I know that working people like me and my fellow UAW members can change the course of politics when we organize,” said Sarah Van Dijk, UAW Local 4811 member in San Diego, CA. “We’ve built a GOTV program unlike anything we’ve done before.” Election Day Is Tuesday. Building Power Doesn’t Stop There. Conversations at the doors are also helping shape the UAW’s working-class agenda for the new Congress in 2027. The concerns and priorities workers share at the doors are informing the union’s broader political work, strengthening the connection between what working people experience on the job and the decisions made by elected officials. Following Election Day, the UAW will take the fight for higher wages, affordable healthcare, a secure retirement and more time off directly to Congress and state legislatures. With the power of its members behind it, the union will hold lawmakers accountable and fight for an economy that puts working people first. Looking ahead to 2028, the UAW is working to build worker power from the shop floor up and fighting to restore the American Dream by ensuring every worker can earn a good living, retire with dignity and have time for family and life outside the job.

articles.title: The Iran War Might Soon Get Catastrophically Worse
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Between all the action around next week’s midterms and Donald Trump’s meddling in Brazilian politics, it’s easy to forget there’s a war going on. But sure enough, Trump’s war on Iran is still humming in the background, and every indication is that it could flare up in a terrible new way very soon. According to multiple reports , Trump has been planning a renewed attack on Iran that is likely to be launched after the midterms, though according to the Wall Street Journal , the president had not yet firmly decided whether he’ll go through with it. The renewed attack, the Journal reports, would be a “short, intense war” that would hit Iranian infrastructure, its munition arsenal, and its nuclear sites, or at least that’s what sources have told the US press. Sen. Chris Murphy, who has been briefed on some of the attack plans, has called them “insane” and said they would lead to “the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law,” which suggests something potentially broader and even more extreme. Funnily enough, a month before any of this reporting was published, Quincy Institute Executive Vice President Trita Parsi had predicted to me that Trump was likely to do this, as a way of trying to end the war on his terms. “Trump has come to a space in his mind in which he believes that he has already tried everything. He’s tried diplomacy. He’s tried sanctions. He’s tried limited war,” Parsi said in mid-September. “The only thing he hasn’t tried is all of those different military threats he issued early on, but never exercised: taking out the desalination plants, taking out Iran’s energy infrastructure, taking one of the islands in the Persian Gulf. I think after the midterms, that is what he’s going to try.” Trump has, not surprisingly, been egged on in this by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in the lead-up to the Israeli election this week repeatedly vowed to restart the war against Iran and “ overthrow ” the remnants of the regime there. But according to the Israeli press, Netanyahu went beyond merely pushing for war: he actively looked to start one with a planned attack on Iran that he was ultimately talked out of. As Netanyahu openly said this week on Twitter/X, he and Israel had a narrow “window of time” to act — specifically, “another two years of Trump to finish the work in Iran.” Netanyahu’s obvious attempts to spark renewed war with Iran briefly became an election issue in Israel, when one of his opponents announced he had requested a treason investigation into the prime minister over his “pressuring the heads of the security establishment to take steps that could create a miscalculation vis-à-vis Iran,” and trying to “drag the state of Israel into war on the eve of elections.” Netanyahu has a history , especially over the past three years, of using war as a means of keeping himself in power, and it’s not hard to see how a war with Iran — particularly one he could sell as being started by Tehran — could give him a popularity boost. Netanyahu’s efforts to do this may not have worked out for the moment, but the currently deadlocked Israeli election result, combined with Trump’s preexisting plans to restart the war as soon as a week from now, could give him another shot at it. If Netanyahu’s opposition remains unable to form a government, he will stay on as caretaker prime minister until the next election, by which point a US war with Iran may well have provided a shot in the arm to his far-right coalition. Playing With Fire But however “insane” and brutal this latest US bombing campaign turns out to be, it’s unlikely to give Trump what he wants: for Tehran to soften its demands and take a deal that’s worse for them and better for him. Trump’s actions — including his repeated violation of agreements and diplomatic protocols, and the sneak attack that killed scores of Iranian officials at the start of the war — have thoroughly delegitimized Iran’s moderates and placed the country firmly in the hands of hard-liners who oppose negotiations, and some of whom do things like move to impeach the country’s more pro-diplomacy foreign minister. These hard-liners believe that any deal Iran strikes with Washington is pointless, because Trump or his successor will just rip it up later regardless. The hard-liners are convinced the only way to ensure both the state’s and the country’s survival is to inflict such costs on the United States and its political leadership that they’ll leave their country alone. They are also, ironically, now looking seriously at actually pursuing a nuclear weapon — a pursuit Iran’s previous supreme leader had, it turns out, been the main roadblock to, until Trump dropped a bomb on his house in February and killed him. Trump still reportedly hopes that using military force will this time stop Iran from making a bomb. But that idea is likely to run into the same problem as before: namely, that Iran’s buried nuclear sites are basically unreachable, even by the largest bombs the United States can drop on them, so he would need to launch a risky ground operation to extract the enriched material that still wouldn’t be guaranteed of success. Look at how costly the vastly less complicated effort to recover a single pilot in April proved, and you start to get a sense of the difficulty with this idea. Meanwhile, Iran’s new hard-line leadership is willing to absorb (or more accurately, willing to let the Iranian people take) a tremendous amount of pain to achieve this, as they have demonstrated. Years of preexisting suffering under US sanctions and a rally-’round-the-flag effect that has seen anti-government dissent evaporate means life in Iran is persisting in the face of widespread shortages, nearly 90 percent inflation, and at least $270 billion worth of destroyed infrastructure. So what would a “short, intense war” on Iran actually do, then? Besides the human toll on ordinary Iranians just trying to live their lives, it would likely mean even worse blowback on everyone else, the United States included. Like Trump, Iran’s leaders have military cards they haven’t played yet, and they are openly threatening much worse retaliation this time if they’re attacked again. Iranian officials have threatened to make the war “longer and in a wider geographical area,” and to inflict a “devastating impact” on energy markets, aiming to shove the world into outright recession and create a large-scale refugee crisis. Surrounding oil facilities, ports, pipelines, refineries, power grids, and even desalination plants have been mentioned as targets. This would be devastating for — and in the case of power grids and desalination plants, existentially threatening to — life in the Gulf states, whose economies have already been battered by the war. This is why a host of Iran’s neighbors, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, have been desperately holding talks with Tehran to try to stop what might be the most devastating round of an already regionally destructive war, so far with no tangible results. But it’s not just Iran’s neighbors who will bear the brunt of this. Iran’s leaders specifically named as targets the undersea cables that carry internet traffic and the trillions of dollars of infrastructure in the region that the US artificial intelligence industry relies on, including data centers. That industry, which Trump is heavily relying on to prop up the US economy, is already showing serious signs of strain in the face of mounting financial losses and growing investor skepticism. Major damage to critical infrastructure and resulting market disruption risks adding further strain on an industry that many already fear is a bubble waiting to pop. In its recent initial public offering prospectus , AI firm Anthropic specifically mentioned the fact that “armed conflict” could damage or destroy data centers and other infrastructure as one of its risk factors, a warning that other industry players have made . More ominously, a senior Iranian security official has also named “US political targets” as potentially fair game. Recall, too, that Iran is widely believed to be the culprit behind months of cyberattacks on a variety of US infrastructure, including water systems . If either of these is part of Iran’s next retaliatory move, it would not only cause intense chaos and suffering for the US public but potentially trigger a dangerous escalation spiral. Vice President J. D. Vance has reportedly now reached out to Iran’s hard-line top security chief to resuscitate peace talks. Given everything laid out above, this would be wise. The Choice Is Clear The trouble is that the two parties here remain a canyon apart. Iranian leadership views it as effectively suicide to budge from the terms they agreed to earlier this year, while Trump has been led to view those terms as a personal humiliation, so he keeps trying and failing to bomb or blockade his way to a more favorable deal after the fact. There is also the wild card of Netanyahu, who has already more than once tried to single-handedly torpedo a Trump-Iran deal by bombing Lebanon and violating one of Iran’s core demands. The White House now is certain that Iran is on the brink of capitulation, and all it will take is one more push to get it there. In reality, Trump is dealing with an Iran that is more dangerous and less likely to capitulate than ever: not because it has a nuke, but because years of Trump’s own foolish policy choices have turned it into an adversary that sees itself as having nothing to lose — and is acting like it, which is why Iranian leaders are effetively threatening that if they go down, they will take the entire region as well as the global economy with them. Trump and the people around him are looking at next week’s midterms as the moment they will be unshackled from political constraints, freeing them to take the reckless, escalatory measures they were reluctant to take before for fear of voter backlash. If they were smart, they would treat it as freeing them instead to take the deal they had already agreed to, and to just swallow the inevitable political point-scoring and cries of “capitulation” that are, sadly, now just standard whenever any president tries to end a war. But it is clear that there is a dearth of voices around the president that are inclined to tell him this. It is increasingly likely that Trump soon takes a step that will prove even more terrible for the country, for his political party, and his own legacy.
