articles.title: In Trump Country, an Independent Candidate Takes On Big Gas and Big Tech
articles.author: Audrey Carleton
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Jodi Borello taps her phone and glances at her campaign manager with quiet urgency: She agreed to meet with a resident, and the time to leave is approaching. Borello sits on a bench under a pavilion in Allenport, a riverside village outside Pittsburgh, hundreds of feet from the site of an old steel plant that residents fear is destined to become a data center: A natural gas company with an exclusive option for the land expressed an interest in getting into the artificial intelligence business, dizzying the town. It’s early October, and with just a few weeks before the 2026 midterm election, Borello has just a few minutes before she must go back to her campaign duties: After meeting with the voter, she is off to give out yard signs then prepare for a house party the next day before more canvassing, phone banking and handing out signs. Between the tasks, the southwestern Pennsylvania state Senate candidate sat with five Allenport residents, one of whom worked at the shuttered Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel mill and who all now oppose a data center moving in. They identify with different places on the political spectrum. One is a lifelong Reagan Republican; another is a onetime Democrat who lost faith in both parties. But they share a common sentiment: Their trust in state and local government has largely eroded. “I don’t trust any elected officials. I’m sorry, Jodi,” one resident says. Borello laughs, seemingly unfazed. In many ways, Borello might be the ideal candidate for voters like this. She is a onetime Republican, is a near-lifelong resident of the region, and is now running as an independent in deeply conservative Senate District 46 to unseat three-term Republican incumbent state Sen. Camera Bartolotta on a platform to hold corporations accountable, improve economic conditions for working people and cut through political gridlock. This is happening as Democrats strive to flip the chamber to achieve a trifecta in the commonwealth for the first time since 1993 should they maintain control of the governor’s office and the House of Representatives. Their strategy does not include flipping the 46th District, but experts said it’s related. A Borello win could cut into Republican numbers and, in the event of a party tie, give Democrats a majority if the executive branch stays blue and the lieutenant governor is given the power to cast a tie-breaking vote. If the party is successful, it would pave the way for a “ tectonic shift ” for environmental policies that have long stalled out in the natural-resource-heavy Keystone State. It would also make Borello the first registered independent to win a state election there in close to a century . Republicans are now pouring hundreds of thousands of dollars into protecting the GOP incumbent and painting Borello as a far left candidate. Her district, despite once being overwhelmingly Democratic, swung far to the right during the red wave of the 2010s. In 2024, President Donald Trump won more than 62% of the vote in Washington County, where both candidates live. Borello’s home of Washington County is also the second-most heavily fracked county in the second-most prolific natural gas state in the country – the natural gas extraction technique, which blasts drilling fluid deep underground, has been controversial in this area for its correlation to health impacts . The candidate has spent years organizing around environmental justice in the shalefields — first in her personal life, and then professionally . Her opponent Bartolotta has long been pro-gas, a stance easy to glean not just from legislation she’s sponsored and thousands of dollars in campaign contributions from gas industry players, but also from the billboards that line the Pennsylvania Turnpike, which feature her headshot and read: “ Simple Math! PA COAL + NATURAL GAS = POWER & PROSPERITY ” Neither Bartolotta nor her campaign staff responded to Capital & Main’s requests for comment. Bartolotta’s stance on natural resource development in this part of the state has historically been the popular choice. But as proposals for power-hungry data centers have swelled , so has opposition to them, uniting neighbors who would otherwise stand on opposite sides of the energy debate. Now, Borello’s campaign to unseat Bartolotta appears to be more than just a pipe dream. After a dramatic and expensive primary fight, Bartolotta’s Democratic opponent dropped out of the race shortly after the primaries just as Borello announced her candidacy. Borello is a first-time candidate but longtime environmental advocate with a clear anti-data center platform, and experts said she could be uniquely positioned for an upset. “You have a whole bunch of things in place with an independent candidate, which maybe neutralizes some of the negative Democratic brand issues in a district like that,” said Christopher Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University . “It was the bluest of the blue, … and it flipped. … When does it flip again?” The political tides have shifted across the country, recent polls show. Trump’s approval rating has hit record lows as the cost of living rises; paychecks flatline by comparison; and energy bills surge , owing in part to the insatiable demand data centers put on the electrical grid. All the while, the president has doubled down on them. “We were all thinking that it was possible for the state Senate to finally flip control … never even considering a place like the 46th would be in play,” said Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research and director of the Floyd Institute for Public Policy at Franklin & Marshall College. The college’s August poll found that nearly 80% of Pennsylvanians oppose data centers built in their communities. In October, polling from State Navigate , a nonprofit nonpartisan group that works to drive engagement with state legislatures, found the two candidates tied . “If Jodi Borello is able to win the race for the 46th District or make it close,” said David Masur, executive director of the nonprofit environmental group PennEnvironment, “it shows that being an advocate who stands up to powerful interests and wants to protect the local environment from the proliferation of data centers is a potent message.” “Jodi and I are living off of protein balls,” Borello’s campaign manager, Veronica Coptis, joked as the two repositioned themselves under the pavilion in Allenport, her neighbors having departed for the lunch hour. “It’s nonstop,” Borello said. “But there is nothing, absolutely nothing, more important to me than helping people like this, because I went through it.” Borello and Coptis met years prior, when Coptis was executive director of the nonprofit Center for Coalfield Justice , an environmental justice organization serving those left in the wake of the fossil fuel development in southwestern Pennsylvania. Borello moved back to her home county in the 2000s to give her three children the bucolic childhood she remembered fondly, but quickly saw that memory disrupted when the natural gas industry moved into her neighborhood. The daughter of a steelworker-turned-upholstery-maker and a nurse whose family’s roots in the area she believes date back to 1803, Borello has an acute appreciation for what coal offered the region. “If you know anything about coal country, we had a red dog lane,” she said, referring to a red-orange coal byproduct that was once used for driveways and pavement. “I probably shoveled more red dog in my life than a backhoe at a coal mine.” But Borello didn’t anticipate that, after moving back home, she’d find herself on the opposing end of a different energy industry. By 2013, natural gas firm CNX Resources Corp. had drilled 34 fracking wells within one and a half miles of Borello’s home, which led to disruptive noise, bright lights, and air pollution, according to allegations in a lawsuit that Borello and her neighbors filed against the company in 2013. CNX did not respond to Capital & Main’s request for comment. Years later, when the state leveled charges against the company for improperly reporting its emissions – to which the company pleaded no contest and agreed to donate to the community where the mishap took place – it was Borello’s notes that they credited with fueling their investigation. Separately, she also testified in front of a grand jury that led the office of then-Attorney General Josh Shapiro, now governor, to make a series of policy recommendations and condemn state regulators’ handling of the fracking boom. In 2022, Borello joined the Center for Coalfield Justice as a community organizer in Washington County, where she spent her time educating neighbors about their rights and recourse against fracking in the area. (The Center’s recently launched political arm has been a key supporter of Borello’s campaign, as has a so-called dark money-funded group called Independent Candidates Action, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette recently reported . A campaign finance filing also showed she received $2,000 each from Barbara and Carl Page, cofounders of the California-based climate organization Anthropocene Institute, and just over $350,000 from a PAC called Rural People Rising.) Despite her years of environmental work, Borello’s platform does not explicitly include any climate messaging. Instead, she focuses on taking on corporations broadly, which she said are exploiting regions like hers. Related: Amazon Data Center Boom Fueled by Lucrative Tax Break She told nonprofit investigative newsroom Spotlight PA that she wouldn’t caucus with either party if elected — a decision that has drawn criticism for potentially alienating her from coalitions and party resources. But Borello could find herself in a position of distinct importance if elected, said David Hess, former secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and editor of the watchdog environmental blog PA Environment Digest. “If Democrats do take over the Senate, it’s going to be by one seat,” he said. “In which case, I’d be courting her 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to vote for a Democrat to run the Senate.” Borello could also find herself in front of Shapiro again. Since the grand jury report’s publication in 2020, she has been vocal in her disappointment with how few of the former attorney general’s recommendations panned out. Shapiro’s office has blamed the split legislature for the lack of action. If elected, Borello said her first goals would be to push for raising the state’s minimum wage — among the lowest in the nation at $7.25 — pass a moratorium on data centers and offer tax breaks to first responders. Related: The Growing Revolt Against AI Data Centers Is Reshaping Local Politics Twelve years ago , Bartolotta, then a Senate hopeful, sat at a dark-wood desk, stacks of papers to her side, and looked straight into the camera. “I’ve always thought that the way you do your work … is a true reflection of your character,” she began in one of her first videos to voters. She then launched into some of her promises to the taxpayer: not to vote for her own pay raise, not to take a pension and not to accept per diems, the daily business allowances legislators are permitted to claim for expenses involved in visiting Harrisburg for legislative session. She appears to have kept the latter promise, but routinely invoices the state for expenses in amounts that critics contend surpass what she’d get from per diems. Bartolotta was then, as Borello is now, new to the campaign trail. An actress originally from Oregon, Bartolotta cut her teeth doing background roles on shows such as “ Cheers” and “The Love Boat ” in California before moving to southwestern Pennsylvania in 1986 with her late husband, Bruce, and opening a quick lube business. She recently described the transition to Pennsylvania as akin to the scene from “The Wizard of Oz,” when, suddenly, “the doors open, and it’s Technicolor,” she told Edmund Sulkowski on Peters Township Community Television’s “The Dr. Ed Show.” It wasn’t until she learned of high poverty rates in a neighborhood near hers that she opted to run for office, she said. A Republican, she unseated Sen. Tim Solobay, a seven-term Democrat, and ended decades of the party’s stronghold over the seat — though not without controversy. Just before the election in 2014, the incumbent made headlines when he was questioned by police in a murder case. He was never implicated in the case. Bartolotta herself withstood a scandal over ties to a movie production company accused of producing a gory film that was described as “degrading to women.” “I didn’t know until election night, when I won, that I was the first Republican senator to win since 1927,” she told Sulkowski in 2025. “And the first woman ever in history to hold the seat.” Bartolotta’s political journey has followed that of a classic conservative: She’s voted with her party on major bills and championed business interests and Second Amendment rights . At the same time, she has reached across party lines to put solar panels on schools and reform the criminal justice system, while legalizing ride-share services and advancing protections for domestic violence survivors. In 2020, she remarried . Her new husband, Bill DeWeese, was once a Democratic power player in the state as former Speaker of the House who served prison time in 2012 after being convicted of illegally using state resources for political gain. He is now registered as a lobbyist. It was her husband’s time in prison that motivated Bartolotta’s criminal justice reform advocacy, she said . The relationship has led some in her party to question her loyalty to the GOP. The county Republican Party recently passed a vote of no confidence in her for speaking out against Trump’s disparagement of Haitian immigrants in her district. But on issues related to fossil fuels, Bartolotta’s stance has been clear. According to Ballotpedia , she campaigned in 2014 on a promise to “block the [President Barack] Obama Administration’s extreme war on our coal industry.” In 2019, she introduced a bill to limit the appeals process for environmental permits, including those for oil and gas. In 2024, she attempted to pass similar restrictions on appeals for natural gas pipeline permits. Neither one reached a floor vote. “Pennsylvania not only could, but should produce four times the amount of natural gas,” she said at the time, standing in front of energy lobbyists in the state Capitol in 2024 for its annual Natural Gas and Oil Day. “We should be exporting freedom. … We just need to get government the hell out of the way.” The same year, she introduced a bill that would withhold impact fee dollars — a charge levied on natural gas producers distributed to the communities in which they operate — from places that “unreasonably” limit gas development, a move that came three days after the township of Cecil, in her district, adopted a rule requiring 2,500-foot buffer setback between fracking wells and homes. Some viewed Bartolotta’s bill as retaliatory. Bartolotta’s 2026 campaign contributions may offer insight into her political stances. In April, she received $2,500 from a political action committee associated with CNX. In May, she received the same from an employee political action committee for Marathon Petroleum Corp. and in October from the PAC for pipeline company TC Energy Corp., formerly known as TransCanada, days after receiving $2,000 from the PAC for fossil fuel firm The Williams Cos. Inc. She has received $8,500 from Pittsburgh-based natural gas producer EQT, the firm interested in getting into the AI business at the old Allenport steel mill. The company’s president and CEO, Toby Z. Rice, also donated $10,000 to Bartolotta’s campaign. Related: Common Ground of ‘ICE Out’ Movements and the Climate EQT did not respond to requests for comment. She also earned personal income from the natural gas industry, according to mineral rights leases she signed with two natural gas companies – Chesapeake Appalachia, LLC, now Expand Energy, and Rice Drilling B LLC, a subsidiary of EQT – in the years before she took office. Ethics disclosure reports she filed in office show that she still earns income from EQT — at least $1,300 per year, the state’s minimum threshold for reporting outside income. This would normally not cause stir within her district. Bartolotta is one of many people earning natural gas royalties in the area, and her pro-gas stance is one she’s proud of: She cochairs the Senate Gas and Oil Caucus. She glided to reelection by double digits in 2018 , then again without an opponent in 2022 . But critics said she miscalculated her district’s opposition to data centers in 2025, when she introduced a bill to accelerate the permitting process for such facilities. It has yet to be brought up for a vote. She also repeatedly cosponsored a measure to introduce a state sales and use tax subsidy for data centers in the late 2010s that was signed into law in 2021 and is projected to cost the state billions of dollars and serves the likes of Amazon. She has since tried to walk back that stance. It’s not clear whether it’s too late. On the banks of the Monongahela River, as the water’s current gently sways boat docks that float beside colonial houses perched on its shoreline, coal-filled train cars roar along a track that slices through the town. The anticipated data center could be what finally pushes some residents of this community to pick up and leave, they said — their trust in their politicians diminished. Borello doesn’t blame them, but said that she hopes to be the person who restores that trust. Capital & Main

articles.title: Preparing for MAGA’s Worst on Election Day
articles.author: Stephanie Luce
articles.content: Imagine this: Election Day comes and goes. Democrats turn out big and flip a few seats, some by close margins. Forces opposing the increasingly authoritarian drift of the United States breathe a sigh of relief. Before the results are even called, however, Donald Trump declares in a wave of Truth Social posts that Democrats have cheated, the results are fraudulent, and those responsible will be prosecuted and persecuted. By the next day, the claims have spread to congressional Republicans, who vow to seek justice — and, in some cases, vengeance — for the supposed voter fraud. Protesters take to the streets in several cities, demanding that all votes be counted. They call on their representatives to stand behind voters’ democratic wishes. The protests spread, and on November 6, Trump claims that protesters in several cities have gotten out of hand and broken windows. He then declares that Iran has engaged in cyber election interference, thereby invalidating the results of the vote. Trump announces he will send in the National Guard and invoke the Insurrection Act to defend the country against these incursions. Is this scenario likely? It’s hard to say. The midterms are shaping up to be a rout of the Republicans, with Trump and his party facing nearly unprecedented unfavorability and losses so great that even his normal bluster and lies about stolen elections won’t be able to hold his diminishing base. In Brazil this week, Flávio Bolsonaro floated a Trumpian trial balloon by claiming the presidential election was stolen by the Workers’ Party’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but the nearly 4.5-million-vote margin that Lula won by made such mendacity absurd, and Bolsonaro has since fled the country for Miami. But given the antidemocratic drift of the United States over the past decade and since Trump’s second election in particular, this scenario is far from impossible. Indeed, parts of it, like Trump’s denial of the election results, seem all but assured. And as the president feels his mandate in the country (and perhaps his own mental health) slipping away, who knows what a newly desperate Trump will do. He would not be alone in taking such steps. Scholars who study authoritarianism call them an “ authoritarian playbook ”: a set of similar steps leaders like Flávio Bolsonaro’s former president father Jair, former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in Hungary, and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey have taken to consolidate power. It includes going after critics through investigations and harassment, installing loyalists, expanding federal powers, crushing dissent, and deploying military forces on their own citizens. The Trump administration has been moving through the playbook at record speed, from firing federal workers to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shootings to the attacks on Rep. Ilhan Omar. Unions, community and faith organizations, immigrant rights groups, and lawyers have resisted and slowed the attacks, but that hasn’t stopped Trump. His administration has already taken steps to undermine the 2026 midterm elections, attempting to restrict mail ballots, purge voter rolls, and mess with ballots in Alaska . They plan to send ICE to the polls. And Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) has announced plans to try to block the seating of democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier , the likely next House member from New York’s Thirteenth District, while MAGA is building the legal case to do exactly that. The task for socialists is not to vote and defend elections in order to return to the status quo, but to defend basic democratic norms while putting forth a vision of a different future. Lots of people care about elections and will be looking for answers if things go wrong. Socialists cannot sit on the sidelines. We need to challenge racist gerrymandering and minoritarian institutions like the Supreme Court and Senate to weaken the stranglehold of the authoritarian right on the federal government in order to have the opportunity to advance reforms that can establish new social and economic rights. Attacks on elections are tied to attacks on our rights to organize and protest, our rights to independent media, and our rights to engage in the democratic institutions we fought hard to create. And for a growing share of the socialist movement, contesting for governing power via elections is a key part of the strategy. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are set to send seven, and potentially as many as ten, members to Congress; their strategy depends on fair elections that get those members seated so they can build a bloc that pushes for transformative demands. We can’t develop a full plan ahead of time, but we can develop our planning skills under crisis. National organizations and some unions have already been training people on potential election scenarios through versions of “ tabletop exercises ” where organizers role-play different scenarios and develop strategy and tactics together. The more we practice, the easier it might be to respond when a crisis hits. One possible scenario to come out of next week’s election is a state of confusion, where vote counting is challenged or stopped in a state or two, and courts are going back and forth about what to do. This would be similar to what happened in 2000 , when the initial presidential vote count in Florida showed George W. Bush beating Al Gore by only 1,784 votes. Gore called for a recount in some counties, including Miami-Dade. Republican operatives moved quickly to send in staffers to protest outside the recount, eventually rushing the doors and attacking people, resulting in the recount being called off. After more back-and-forth, the case went to the Supreme Court, which called for an end to the recount. Rather than protesting, Democratic Party leaders, including Gore (who would have won in a full recount), accepted the loss. This time around, we need to be ready to respond to ballot and legal confusion without waiting for courts to decide. If we have another Florida-type scenario, such as Republican operatives refusing to count all the ballots in Texas, then socialists and all our allies need to be ready to fight back. People around the country, whether in blue, red, or purple states, can fill the streets and pressure their representatives, especially Democrats, to demand that every vote is counted. Legal observers and traditional election groups are working to protect voter registration, ensure access to polls, and prepare legal challenges. No Kings will be ready to call for mass peaceful marches. May Day Strong is preparing for economic disruption if needed, examining how people can undermine the corporate pillars that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism. There are billionaires and corporations directly profiting from surveillance, ICE contracts, war, and deregulation: they have a material interest in Trump’s success. Some billionaires, such as Peter Thiel and Elon Musk, go beyond that and have an ideological commitment to authoritarianism of various forms. Using the full toolbox of boycotts, sit-ins, slowdowns, walkouts, and strikes, how can we best target the billionaires and corporations who are enabling and profiting from authoritarianism, like Amazon and Jeff Bezos, and how can we encourage others, like Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan Chase and Delta Air Lines , to defect from the authoritarian coalition by making it too costly to stay? A Broad Front Working in a broad front, a wide range of political actors who may oppose Trump’s antidemocratic measures but disagree with us on most everything else, to defeat authoritarianism can be simple on the one hand, because there is one unifying task: build the biggest “we” possible to defeat MAGA. But broad front politics get complicated fast. It means working with mainstream Democrats who often seem more intent on destroying DSA than MAGA. It might mean working with anti-Trump Republicans, who see socialists as the second-biggest threat after authoritarians. And it requires being in alignment with a whole host of organizations that can be annoying or disruptive or way too verbose. Working in a broad front requires patience, education, and skill. But it also opens up the space to work with millions of people who are newly engaged by the real threat MAGA poses to their lives or jobs. As Ash-Lee Henderson reminds us, 89 million people didn’t vote in 2024. People are angry about the cost of living, and many want and need big changes, from Medicare for All to reliable transit to an end to war. The Democratic Party has made little to no effort to acknowledge these 89 million and their frustrations, leaving the job to socialists or right-wing extremists. To stay anchored in a broad front, socialists need nested strategies: a short-term strategy to block the authoritarian right and a longer-term strategy to build the Left. We can do that by emphasizing the capacities we need to build no matter the task: democratic participation, mass training and education on the issues that matter, door-knocking and talking with coworkers, organizing unions and mapping workplaces. We’ll need these skills to defend the midterm results; if we can do them well, we’ll connect with thousands of new people joining the fight — and be in stronger shape to shift from defense to offense. Since the start of the second Trump administration, many unions, DSA chapters, and community organizations have had to develop the ability for rapid response against the federal government’s attacks on our neighbors. We have called protests against federal workforce union busting, developed mutual aid networks to support immigrants, and trained ourselves in direct action. By getting more organized at a block-by-block level, we can prepare for the possibility of Republicans seriously contesting the results of our elections and make sure we are ready to organize more workers who know that we need a real voice not just in our workplaces but in our political system too. Building these muscles puts us in better shape for actions in 2028, including influencing the presidential primaries and election, and a potential May 1, 2028, national strike. Our tasks: Vote. Get trained on noncooperation and strike readiness . Sign a pledge to defend the elections through targeted actions on corporations and elected officials. If things get messy, be ready to help coworkers and neighbors make sense of the moment and invite them into the organizations that are fighting for a better world. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Dolores Huerta Taught a Generation How to Organize
articles.author: David Bacon
articles.content: When I came back from a solidarity work brigade in Cuba in the 1970s, I landed in New York City with no place to sleep. I called Lori Huerta, a friend from California, and daughter of Dolores Huerta (1930–2026), cofounder of the United Farm Workers (UFW). Not only did I get space on the floor of the NYC grape boycott headquarters, but Dolores and her partner, Richard, César Chávez’s brother, took us out to eat. Over pizza I enthused about the island. I had stars in my eyes, for both Cuba and Dolores, and still do. I went to work for the UFW as an organizer a few months later. At the beginning of the Iraq War, Huerta marches with actor Danny Glover and an enormous crowd demanding that the troops be brought home. (Courtesy David Bacon) Over the years, long after I had left the UFW and worked for other unions and then as a photojournalist, I would see Dolores again and again. Going to Watsonville to cover the organizing drives of strawberry workers or to Salinas for the strikes in the vegetable fields, I knew she’d be there. It was a profound experience to watch her in union contract negotiations — this diminutive woman facing off against the beefy growers across the table — and see the sense of power it gave workers. For Dolores and Eliseo Medina, another of my teachers, being a good organizer was the bottom line — doing what the workers needed. María Elena Durazo, who came from a farmworker family to head the Los Angeles Labor Federation and now sits in the legislature, remembered, “In that world of rural California, it was the grape strike and the boycotts that taught us that the only way to end poverty and injustice was to organize together. It was the United Farm Workers who taught us that, and Dolores was the best teacher among many good ones.” Returning from Iraq, where I photographed workers after the 2003 US invasion, I took her picture in the front line of marchers against the war. When we were in Sacramento trying to stop the anti-immigrant, anti–affirmative action, anti-bilingual initiatives, she was the first to speak out. There was often tension in the UFW about radical politics, and being called a “red” was sometimes the route out the door. Fear of saying anything that could lead to getting fired enabled César Chávez to exert such power that even otherwise aggressive and militant organizers and workers, like Dolores, didn’t challenge him, whether about sexual abuse or political purges. Abuse is a fact in other unions I’ve belonged to, and progressive leaders have stayed quiet there too. We have to confront this system of male supremacy directly, and I know she believed this. At the start of the Immigrant Workers Freedom Ride in San Francisco, Huerta and hotel workers marched to demand immigrant reform. (Courtesy David Bacon) Her relationship with the Democratic Party was complicated. She supported some movements for political independence in the 1990s while also campaigning for mainstream Democrats. As the union’s political director, she got the California legislature to pass a union recognition bill far better than the National Labor Relations Act, as well as pesticide protections and overtime that don’t even exist in other states. Randy Villegas, our hope for breaking the MAGA stranglehold on the southern San Joaquin Valley, is someone she’s had her eye on for years. You could call her a realist. Four years ago I walked with Dolores from Poplar to Delano, California, in honor of Larry Itliong, who started the 1965 grape strike and boycott there. She was ninety-one then, and I had a hard time keeping up. She sent me a note afterward that ended, “Sí Se Puede con El Rojo Tocino.” It was a beautiful joke. Huerta marches with San Joaquin Valley farmworkers and activists, celebrating the birthday of Larry Itliong, the Filipino leader who started the 1965 grape strike. (Courtesy David Bacon) “Sí Se Puede” are three words we all use now, but she invented this confident way of saying “Yes We Can!” “Tocino” was the nickname the union gave me in the years I worked as an organizer — it means “bacon,” my last name. And calling me “El Rojo,” or “The Red,” in this way honored my politics. So when she called me El Rojo Tocino, I thought, “What a compliment!” I hope I live up to it. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
