articles.title: Uniting the Left
articles.author: Sharon Kyle, Eric Mann, Vincent De Stefano, Dick Price, Robert Corsini
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. What happens when a room full of people who want to change the world cannot agree on how to change it? That question hung over a spirited roundtable discussion titled "Uniting the Left" at the 2026 Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4 at California State University, Los Angeles. The gathering brought together activists, organizers, political thinkers and representatives of progressive organizations to confront a problem that has frustrated the American left for generations: Despite widespread dissatisfaction with political and economic conditions, progressive movements remain fragmented, often struggling to translate their collective numbers into political power. The panel featured Ben Cohen, co-founder of Ben & Jerry's; veteran civil rights organizer Eric Mann; LA Progressive publisher and Left Coast Forum co-founder Sharon Kyle; former Santa Monica Rent Control Board chair Ericka Lesley; and longtime peace and social justice activist Vincent De Stefano. Their common objective was straightforward: explore the possibility of creating a united front among organizations participating in the forum. But as the discussion unfolded, it became apparent that agreement on the need for unity was considerably easier than agreement on what unity would require. Can There Be Unity Without Racial Justice? Kyle opened the discussion by questioning why progressive organizations, despite their numbers and shared concerns, have been unable to exercise greater influence over national policy. Sharon Kyle Pointing to federal layoffs, attacks on diversity initiatives, reductions in public assistance and aggressive immigration enforcement, she argued that the left needs something more consequential than expressions of solidarity. It needs power. Kyle suggested that racial division has historically enabled concentrated economic power to survive by preventing working people from recognizing and acting upon their common interests. Drawing on Republican strategist Lee Atwater's notorious explanation of the Southern Strategy, she described how explicitly racist political appeals evolved into seemingly race-neutral language involving taxes, government spending and social programs. The resulting policies, she argued, can preserve racial hierarchies even when politicians avoid explicitly mentioning race. For Kyle, the question was not simply how organizations could unite around shared economic interests, but whether they could meaningfully confront the racial divisions that have repeatedly undermined efforts at solidarity. Eric Mann Mann, director of the Labor/Community Strategy Center and a veteran of the civil rights movement, challenged the assumption that the fundamental political struggle could be reduced to the 99 percent against the wealthiest 1 percent. He argued that racism is not merely a tool wielded by economic elites against an otherwise unified working class. White Americans, including members of the working class, have historically participated in and benefited from systems of racial domination. Mann's analysis centered the United States' history of settler colonialism, slavery and imperialism. Drawing on his decades of organizing, including work with the Congress of Racial Equality and in Black communities during the 1960s, he argued that the progressive movement must place Black political power at the center of its strategy. "We don't need DEI, although it's good. We need Black power," Mann declared. He also questioned whether electoral victories, even those involving politicians he admires, could produce fundamental transformation without stronger independent social movements. For Mann, the immediate priority was not capturing the presidency but building organizations capable of advancing demands that conventional electoral politics routinely excludes. Ben Cohen Offers a Plan for 2028 While Mann emphasized the limitations of electoral politics, Ben Cohen presented a proposal designed to influence the next presidential election. Introducing an initiative he called "Citizens in Search of a Candidate," Cohen described a broad, multi-issue people's platform built around demands that already enjoy substantial public support. Ben Cohen His premise was that progressive organizations have divided themselves into separate movements for racial justice, environmental protection, immigrant rights, economic equality, housing and peace. Each movement struggles against powerful institutional opponents, yet they often fail to combine their strength. "None of us can succeed alone. We can all succeed together," Cohen told the gathering. His proposal would bring organizations together to develop a common platform encompassing such priorities as removing money from politics, establishing living wages, expanding affordable housing and childcare, providing universal healthcare, protecting the environment, ending endless wars and redirecting excessive military spending toward human needs. Rather than beginning with a preferred presidential candidate, the movement would first establish its demands and then seek to influence candidates competing for public support. Cohen envisioned a national listening tour, media campaigns, participation by social media influencers and potentially millions of people signing onto the platform. The objective was to make ordinary people, rather than corporate donors, the driving force behind the political agenda. Cohen also challenged the familiar argument that the United States cannot afford expansive social programs. He introduced a video using Oreo cookies to illustrate the scale of military spending and what comparable resources could accomplish if redirected toward housing, education, healthcare and other public needs. The presentation offered a vivid illustration of the choices underlying federal budget priorities. But Cohen's proposal also raised a difficult question: Could organizations with fundamentally different political analyses agree on a common platform without suppressing their disagreements? Representation Is Not the Same as Power Ericka Lesley brought a different perspective to the discussion, drawing on her experience as a Black woman in local government and as someone who had personally experienced homelessness. Erika Lesley Lesley, who served on the Santa Monica Rent Control Board and became its first Black woman chair, described the obstacles she encountered while attempting to represent communities historically excluded from political decision-making. Her message challenged organizations that celebrate diversity while failing to support the leadership of people of color. "We can't just request people of color's labor without also supporting their leadership," she said. Lesley argued that people who identify racial inequities can themselves become targets of hostility, including within institutions that profess commitments to fairness and inclusion. Her critique extended beyond electoral representation. She described wage theft, union busting and failures of solidarity among organizations supposedly pursuing similar objectives. "We are not in a time of allyship. We are in a time of co-conspiracy," she declared. The distinction was significant. Allyship can imply sympathy or support from a distance. What Lesley called for was active participation in struggles against injustice, including a willingness to challenge established power relationships. She also questioned why some international conflicts command sustained attention among American progressives while others receive comparatively little discussion. Pointing to violence in Ethiopia, she argued that African suffering should not become secondary to struggles elsewhere. Her intervention illustrated a recurring problem for coalition-building: Even organizations committed to universal human rights may differ sharply over which crises deserve immediate attention and resources. Finding Common Ground Without Erasing Differences Vincent De Stefano, a longtime activist associated with Assange Defense and Amnesty International, emphasized the potential strength of a movement willing to set aside sectarian disputes. The political and economic establishment, he suggested, possesses enormous advantages in wealth, media influence and institutional power. Ordinary people, however, possess numbers. Vincent De Stefano De Stefano argued that organizations could build greater influence by identifying common demands, including healthcare, opposition to war and civil liberties, even where participants disagree on broader political questions. The audience soon demonstrated both the appeal and complexity of that approach. Former Santa Monica Mayor Mike Feinstein argued that a progressive platform would accomplish little without changes to the electoral system itself. He advocated proportional representation and ranked-choice voting, suggesting that structural reforms could allow independent political movements to compete more effectively. Other participants proposed Social Security protection as a potentially unifying demand, challenged the progressive movement's approach to nuclear energy, called for stronger attention to African conflicts and urged greater leadership by people of color. One participant warned that creating another nonprofit organization would not solve the left's underlying problems. Instead, he urged greater investment in existing grassroots organizations and stronger opportunities for young activists to assume leadership. These contributions underscored the central dilemma: A movement expansive enough to include different constituencies must also develop ways to make decisions when those constituencies disagree. An especially revealing exchange followed an audience member's question about the possibility of building alliances across political differences. Mann responded that the purpose of a united front should not be to persuade everyone to abandon their political positions. "Nobody should try to win the argument," he said. Instead, he urged participants to respect their differences, listen to one another and identify opportunities for cooperation. That may have been one of the discussion's most practical observations. Unity need not require ideological uniformity. But it does require a willingness to recognize where cooperation is possible—and where disagreements cannot simply be wished away. From Conversation to Political Power The discussion did not conclude with the announcement of a formal united front, an agreed organizational structure or a binding set of commitments among participating groups. What emerged instead was a clearer picture of the work such an undertaking would require. Cohen's proposed platform offered a possible mechanism for organizing around common demands. Mann insisted that independent movements and the struggle against racial domination remain central. Lesley challenged progressives to examine whose leadership they support in practice. Kyle pressed participants to confront racial division as an obstacle to collective power. De Stefano emphasized the practical necessity of cooperation. Together, their contributions exposed a problem that cannot be resolved by simply assembling more organizations under a common banner. A united front would have to determine how decisions are made, whose priorities receive attention, how leadership is shared, how disagreements are resolved and what participating organizations are actually prepared to do together. Near the session's conclusion, former Ohio State Senator Nina Turner briefly addressed the gathering, reinforcing the importance of ordinary people taking responsibility for political change. "Nobody with a special title is coming to save us," she reminded the audience. The remark captured the challenge facing the participants. The American left does not lack organizations, ideas, grievances or committed activists. What it has struggled to develop is the collective capacity to turn those resources into sustained political power. The Left Coast Forum's "Uniting the Left" discussion offered no easy formula for overcoming that weakness. But it accomplished something important: It placed the movement's internal divisions, strategic disagreements and unresolved questions of leadership squarely on the table. Perhaps that is where meaningful unity must begin—not with declarations that differences no longer matter, but with the difficult work of confronting them. Watch the full discussion: Uniting the Left — Left Coast Forum 2026 .

articles.title: UAW Stands Against Divide and Conquer Politics in Michigan Senate Race
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: The United Auto Workers stands against the disgusting divide-and-conquer politics being used in the Michigan Senate race against the candidate of the working class, Abdul El-Sayed. When our members endorsed El-Sayed early in this race, it was because of his aspirational vision for what is possible when we come together and fight for all of us. We are living in a time of the worst wealth inequality in our nation’s history, a time when working-class people are struggling to live. For over 90 years, our union has fought for a united working class that can take on the billionaire class and their corporate lapdogs like Mike Rogers. For over 90 years, billionaires have tried to divide us by race, religion, and more, to keep us weak and fighting amongst ourselves, instead of fighting our common enemies. And for over 90 years, we have rejected division in the name of civil and human rights, solidarity, unity, and common cause across race, religion, and gender. And in Michigan, we have proved time and time again that it is possible for working people to prevail over their divide and conquer tactics. That is how we birthed the American Dream and created the middle class, and it is what will win the future. On Tuesday, we are going to prove it again, when we send Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate and send Mike Rogers back to Florida. This is a “Which Side Are You On?” Moment for all working-class Michiganders. The UAW – Black, Brown, White, Jewish, Christian, Muslim – is on the side of justice and working-class unity, and we are proud to stand with our next Senator, Abdul El-Sayed.

articles.title: From Daryl Gates to Digital Surveillance: Is Los Angeles Really Protecting Immigrants?
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the 2026 Los Angeles mayoral race, City Councilmember Nithya Raman has accused Mayor Karen Bass of failing to adequately protect immigrant communities from federal immigration enforcement. That is a serious charge. It deserves serious examination. But Raman's criticism has raised another question, one that connects directly to Los Angeles's history of policing. During a mayoral debate, Raman invoked the LAPD's 1979 Special Order 40 as a model of immigrant protection, describing the policy associated with the Daryl Gates era as a “gold standard.” She subsequently clarified that she was praising the policy, not Gates himself. That distinction matters. So does the extraordinary difference between the world of 1979 and the world of 2026. If we are going to evaluate which candidate can best protect immigrant communities, we must look beyond historical comparisons and political accusations. We must examine how government power operates today—and whether our leaders understand the technological capabilities of the institutions they oversee. What Special Order 40 Actually Did Special Order 40 was adopted in 1979, during Mayor Tom Bradley's administration, when Daryl Gates was chief of the LAPD. It prohibited officers from initiating police action solely to determine someone's immigration status. The purpose was important. Immigrant residents needed confidence that reporting crimes or cooperating with police would not automatically expose them to immigration enforcement. But Special Order 40 was not an absolute prohibition on cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Nor did it eliminate the broader problems associated with policing under Gates. As discussed in Part 1 , Gates presided over an era marked by aggressive policing, Operation Hammer, and profound mistrust between the LAPD and Black communities. A policy offering meaningful protections to immigrants could coexist with practices that inflicted serious harm on other populations. That contradiction deserves recognition. But there is another problem with treating Special Order 40 as a contemporary standard. It was developed for a world in which the collection, storage, and exchange of personal information were far more limited. Technology has fundamentally changed what cooperation between government agencies can mean. The Difference Between 1979 and 2026 In 1979, police generally gathered information about someone's identity or movements through direct encounters, investigations, and comparatively limited record systems. Today, government agencies can collect, retain, search, and exchange enormous quantities of information. Automated license plate readers record vehicle movements. Booking fingerprints can enter national databases accessible to multiple agencies. Commercial databases can assemble information about people's addresses, associations, and activities. Information collected for one purpose can become useful for another. An LAPD officer does not necessarily have to question someone about immigration status—or personally contact an ICE agent—for information collected through local policing to become accessible to federal authorities. That does not mean every database connection constitutes an unlawful disclosure. It means effective immigrant protection requires more than restrictions on individual officers' conduct. A city can comply with an older policy while leaving residents exposed to dangers its authors could scarcely have imagined. That is why I find Raman's invocation of Special Order 40 as a contemporary “gold standard” inadequate. The question is whether Los Angeles's protections have kept pace with the institutions they are intended to restrain. The Surveillance Warnings Los Angeles Has Already Received These concerns are not speculative. For years, the ACLU of Southern California and the Stop LAPD Spying Coalition have documented and challenged the LAPD's expanding surveillance capabilities. In litigation reported in 2017, the ACLU and Electronic Frontier Foundation documented that the LAPD and Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department were collecting approximately three million license plate scans weekly and had accumulated roughly half a billion records. Those historical figures reveal the extraordinary scale surveillance had already reached nearly a decade ago. The records concerned ordinary motorists, not simply people suspected of crimes. Such databases can reveal where people travel, worship, seek medical treatment, or participate in political activity. Stop LAPD Spying has examined what it calls the architecture of surveillance : the interconnected technologies, databases, agencies, and institutional relationships through which police gather and use information. Its research has connected data-driven policing to racialized enforcement and the displacement of marginalized communities. In its report Automating Banishment , the coalition examines relationships among policing, surveillance, real estate development, and the regulation of urban space. The coalition has also raised concerns about real-time crime centers, automated license plate readers, and private surveillance vendors. Not every allegation made by advocates has been conclusively established. Nor does every surveillance technology necessarily violate the law. But Los Angeles has received detailed warnings about these capabilities for years. That history creates responsibilities for elected officials. When evaluating Bass, we should ask what her administration has done to investigate these concerns, independently assess surveillance systems, and ensure compliance with city protections. When evaluating Raman, we should ask whether her proposals address the broader surveillance infrastructure or only particular relationships with federal immigration authorities. Both candidates should explain what they would do when a surveillance technology cannot be adequately controlled. Would they restrict it, suspend it, or end the city's use of it? Raman's Criticism of Bass Deserves Scrutiny Raman has accused the Bass administration of allowing LAPD practices that potentially expose immigrants to federal enforcement. She has raised concerns about information sharing and questioned whether the city has done enough to prevent cooperation with ICE. Those concerns deserve examination. But political accountability requires factual precision. Reporting has raised questions about LAPD booking fingerprints entering national systems accessible to immigration authorities. That is troubling, particularly if information collected during routine policing can later facilitate immigration enforcement. But federal access to information does not, by itself, establish that LAPD officials deliberately transmitted it to ICE in violation of city policy. Similarly, concerns about automated license plate readers require examining who controls the information, who can access it, how long it is retained, and whether vendors or other agencies can disclose it. The LAPD has said it found no evidence that its license plate reader information was shared with immigration enforcement agencies. That assertion deserves independent verification. It should neither be accepted uncritically nor disregarded without contrary evidence. Raman is entitled to challenge Bass. Holding an incumbent mayor accountable for the police department is precisely what a challenger should do. But which practices does Raman believe violate sanctuary protections? What evidence supports those allegations? What corrective measures would she implement? Bass must answer equally specific questions. Has her administration independently audited information-sharing systems? Has it examined vulnerabilities created by technology vendors? How does it verify compliance? What consequences follow violations? These questions matter more than competing claims about historical commitment. What Los Angeles Has Actually Done Los Angeles has not been standing still. In 2023, Councilmembers Raman, Eunisses Hernandez, and Hugo Soto-Martínez introduced a motion directing the city to develop stronger sanctuary protections. Following Donald Trump's reelection in November 2024, Bass worked with City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto to accelerate the legislation. The City Council adopted the ordinance, and Bass signed it into law in December 2024. The ordinance restricted the use of city personnel, property, resources, and information to support federal immigration enforcement, subject to legal exceptions. In July 2025, Bass issued Executive Directive No. 12, instructing city departments to reinforce those protections. Both Raman and Bass deserve recognition for their contributions. Raman helped initiate the legislative effort. Bass helped accelerate its completion, signed the ordinance, and subsequently directed its implementation. But adopting protections and ensuring their effectiveness are different responsibilities. The mayor oversees city departments, appoints leadership, and influences enforcement priorities. The City Council also exercises legislative, budgetary, and oversight authority. Neither candidate can reasonably claim that immigrant protection is solely the other's responsibility. And neither should be judged solely by legislation supported or directives issued. The question is whether those measures work. A sanctuary designation cannot substitute for effective administration, meaningful oversight, and adequate resources. The Foothold: When Surveillance Expands Beyond Its Original Targets This is where my Foothold Theory becomes relevant. The theory begins with a proposition: Those seeking to accumulate power often find their easiest opportunities among populations least able to resist. They are the low-hanging fruit. Immigrants facing detention or deportation may have limited ability to challenge government practices. Public officials can justify extraordinary measures by portraying targeted populations as dangerous, undeserving, or outside the circle of people whose rights merit protection. When the public accepts those justifications, those exercising power may gain more than an immediate advantage. They gain a foothold. In surveillance, that foothold may take the form of databases, expanded monitoring capabilities, information-sharing arrangements, or weakened expectations of privacy. Once established, those systems need not remain confined to the populations originally used to justify them. A system capable of tracking an immigrant's movements can track a citizen's movements. A database revealing where one vulnerable population lives, works, or travels can reveal the same information about others. And a surveillance capability created under one administration can be inherited by another with different priorities and fewer restraints. This does not mean every official supporting surveillance intends to abuse it. But it would be dangerous to assume that the first population subjected to an intrusive government practice will necessarily be the last. That is the difference between examining surveillance as a collection of technologies and examining it as an accumulation of institutional power. What the Miner's Canary Is Telling Us In Part 2, I described the disappearance of Black Los Angeles through the metaphor of the Miner's Canary. When the canary began to suffer, miners knew the air had become dangerous. The warning was not simply about the bird. It was about conditions threatening everyone. Immigrant communities may now be revealing another danger. When government can monitor movements, assemble personal information, and connect databases across agencies, those capabilities create risks extending beyond immigration enforcement. The Miner's Canary identifies the warning. My Foothold Theory asks who is accumulating power, how they are doing it, and what prevents them from expanding its use. Together, these ideas explain why defending vulnerable populations is not merely an act of compassion. It is also an act of collective self-preservation. Martin Luther King Jr. warned that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.” I understand that warning not only as a moral principle but as a practical observation about power. Those willing to exploit one population's vulnerability have not necessarily demonstrated that they will respect the rights of others when circumstances change. Why should we assume they will stop? What a Mayor Must Understand The debate over immigration enforcement returns us to the central question running through this series. What understanding should we require of someone seeking to serve as mayor of Los Angeles? The mayor cannot control federal immigration law or prevent every federal enforcement action. But the mayor can direct city departments, appoint leadership, propose budgets, oversee compliance, and work with the City Council to strengthen safeguards. Those responsibilities require more than good intentions. They require understanding how modern institutions accumulate information, how technology expands their capabilities, and how authority granted for one purpose can be used for another. Raman is right to demand accountability from Bass. But invoking a policy adopted in 1979 does not establish what protections are adequate in 2026. Bass is right to point to the city's sanctuary commitments. But issuing directives does not establish that those protections are effective in practice. Both candidates must explain how they would identify and close gaps between policy and enforcement. Both must demonstrate an understanding of the technological realities confronting immigrant communities. And both must recognize that inadequate safeguards threaten more than those currently targeted by immigration enforcement. The measure of leadership is not merely whether a mayor supports immigrant rights in principle. It is whether the mayor understands the powers threatening those rights and can use the authority of the office to restrain them. The Danger of Failing to Recognize Power Los Angeles's history offers an important lesson. Government power can expand through policies, practices, and technologies that initially appear limited in purpose. The most vulnerable may experience the consequences first. But they are not necessarily the last. This is why historical ignorance is dangerous in political leadership. A mayor who does not understand how institutions acquire and exercise power may fail to recognize new threats until they are deeply embedded. A mayor who disregards vulnerable communities may overlook the warnings those communities provide. And a public that assumes those warnings concern only immigrants, Black residents, or other marginalized populations may discover too late that the protections it neglected were protections everyone needed. The question confronting Los Angeles is not whether Special Order 40 was progressive in 1979. It was. The question is whether our leaders understand what it takes to protect people in 2026. If Los Angeles cannot prevent powerful institutions from using modern surveillance systems against its most vulnerable residents, what assurance do the rest of us have that those systems will not eventually be used against us? That is the question both candidates should be required to answer. Part 3 of the four-part series “Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? History, Race, Immigration, and Political Responsibility.” Part 4 examines how U.S. foreign and economic policies have contributed to migration, and what responsibility American leaders bear for the consequences. Sources and Further Reading Los Angeles Times: Bass and Raman Trade Accusations Over ICE—and Daryl Gates City of Los Angeles: Executive Directive No. 12, Standing United—A Proud City of Immigrants Los Angeles City Attorney: Court Dismisses Federal Challenge to Sanctuary-City Ordinance

articles.title: UAW Members Drive Ambitious Political Operation to Oust Commissioner Responsible for 8-Month Strike
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: After months of organizing that began in the summer, the UAW is on track to knock the doors of tens of thousands of union members in Lorain County to turn out the vote against County Commissioner Jeff Riddell. Since February 18, UAW Local 2192 members from Lorain County Job and Family Services have been out on strike due to Commissioners like Riddell refusing to bargain in good faith and denying the $1 per hour raises the workforce needs to afford to survive today’s affordability crisis. Already the longest public-sector strike in Ohio’s history, the Lorain Country Job and Family Services strike is weeks from becoming the longest public-sector strike in U.S. history. In May’s primary, Riddell defeated his Republican opponent by only 18 votes – after initially making it into the seat in 2022 by just over 100 votes. “We have dozens of UAW canvassers in the field across Lorain County knocking doors to elect Amy Acton, Sherrod Brown, and Carolyn White for Lorain County Commissioner,” said Gina Jones, UAW Local 2192 bargaining committee co-chair and case worker on strike at Lorain County Job and Family Services. “Voters in Lorain County are sick of elected officials like Jeff Riddell who are bad at their jobs. We’re facing too much of an affordability crisis that all of us are hurt by. Our strike is the clearest example of how important it is to elect people who represent the interests of the working class. We need to elect candidates of all levels of government that aren’t driven by big money interests.” UAW canvassers knocking doors in Lorain County come from various workplaces represented by the UAW in the area. UAW Local 2192 members on strike during the week have been volunteering on Saturdays to join the large-scale canvass walks to reach out to UAW voters and their families about why Commissioner Jeff Riddell needs to be ousted on November 3.

articles.title: Where Did Black Los Angeles Go? The Disappearance of a Community That Built the City
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Part Two of Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? Los Angeles celebrates its diversity. Its leaders routinely invoke the contributions of the many communities that have shaped the city. But something extraordinary has happened to one of those communities. Black Los Angeles has been disappearing. In 1980, approximately 496,000 Black people lived in Los Angeles, representing nearly 17 percent of its population. By 2020, that number had fallen to approximately 367,000, or about 9 percent. The city lost more than one-quarter of its Black population even as its overall population grew. Those numbers represent families leaving neighborhoods, businesses losing customers, churches losing congregants, and communities losing political influence. But the disappearance of Black Los Angeles is more than a demographic story. I believe it was an early warning of the economic insecurity now threatening millions of Americans. And the warning concerns not only what happened to Black Angelenos, but also what their experience reveals about how power and wealth accumulate. A Community That Helped Build Los Angeles People of African ancestry were among the city's original settlers in 1781. Of the 44 settlers who established the Spanish pueblo on Indigenous land, 26 had some African ancestry. Generations later, Black migrants from the South helped transform Los Angeles into an industrial powerhouse. They worked in aircraft manufacturing, defense production, transportation, and other industries while confronting discrimination in employment and housing. Black entrepreneurs established businesses, newspapers, churches, and cultural institutions. Central Avenue became a nationally significant center of Black music and commerce. South Los Angeles and Crenshaw became centers of political organizing and community life. Black leaders, including Mayor Tom Bradley, helped reshape city government. Black Angelenos were among the people who built modern Los Angeles. So why did so many leave? When Economic Security Disappeared For much of the twentieth century, industrial employment offered working-class families a path toward stability. Many jobs provided wages and benefits that made homeownership and a measure of financial security possible. Union contracts established wage scales, seniority protections, grievance procedures, and rules governing promotions and dismissal. Unions were not free of racial discrimination. But where Black workers gained meaningful representation, collective bargaining helped limit employers' ability to make arbitrary decisions. As manufacturing jobs disappeared, that economic foundation weakened. Factories closed, production moved elsewhere, and technological changes reduced demand for labor. Employers and policymakers also embraced arrangements that diminished workers' bargaining power. Black workers, already disadvantaged by discriminatory employment practices and unequal access to accumulated wealth, were especially vulnerable. For families with limited savings, losing a stable job could mean losing the ability to remain in Los Angeles. Meanwhile, housing costs continued rising. Many Black families moved to the Antelope Valley, the Inland Empire, and other communities where homes were more affordable. Some left voluntarily in pursuit of new opportunities. Others faced economic pressures that made remaining increasingly difficult. The distinction matters. But so does the larger pattern: a community that helped build Los Angeles was finding it harder to afford living here. Housing Discrimination Did Not End When It Became Illegal Housing discrimination compounded these pressures. For decades, racially restrictive covenants, discriminatory lending, and exclusionary real estate practices prevented Black families from accessing neighborhoods and building housing wealth available to white families. But it would be misleading to suggest that discrimination ended when fair-housing laws were enacted and only its economic consequences remained. The discrimination itself continued. I know this firsthand. In 1973, when I was 16, I participated in a high school experiment in Lakewood, California, designed to test racial discrimination in apartment rentals. A white female classmate and I posed as recent college graduates seeking apartments. We visited the same four apartment complexes separately, with me going first. At every location, I was told the apartment had already been rented. When my white classmate visited those same properties, all four accepted her application. At one complex, the manager who had told me the apartment was unavailable invited her inside to see the vacant unit. This happened five years after Congress passed the Fair Housing Act. The managers had been polite to me. Their discrimination was concealed beneath ordinary courtesy. My classmates were excited that our experiment had produced compelling evidence. But I was beginning to understand something far more personal. We had documented obstacles I could expect to encounter throughout my life. My white classmate received opportunities denied to me, although our supposed qualifications were identical. She had done nothing to earn that advantage. I had done nothing to deserve the disadvantage. The experience taught me that making discrimination illegal does not eliminate the willingness to discriminate. And when discriminatory conduct goes unchallenged, those responsible can continue benefiting from it. Black Los Angeles Was the Miner's Canary In the book, The Miner's Canary , Lani Guinier and Gerald Torres used the canary once carried into coal mines as a metaphor for racial inequality. When the canary showed signs of distress, miners knew the air was becoming dangerous. The problem was not confined to the bird. It was a warning to everyone in the mine. I believe Black Los Angeles served a similar function. For decades, Black families experienced disappearing industrial jobs, weakening labor protections, persistent housing discrimination, and rising living costs. Many eventually left the city. Today, in 2026, Americans across racial lines are confronting versions of that same insecurity. Stable employment no longer guarantees financial stability. Homeownership is increasingly difficult for younger generations. Housing costs consume household incomes while workers struggle to keep wages aligned with living expenses. The experiences are not identical. Black Angelenos faced particular forms of racial exclusion that cannot be erased by comparisons with broader economic hardship. But the underlying vulnerabilities should look familiar. The warning signs were visible long before economic insecurity became so widespread. Why didn't more Americans recognize them? The Foothold: How Power Gains More Power Martin Luther King Jr. wrote in his Letter from Birmingham Jail that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.” For much of my life, I understood those words primarily as a moral appeal: we should care about injustice even when it happens to someone else. I have come to understand King's warning in a more expanded way. It is also a warning about the nature of those who perpetrate injustice. People willing to exploit others, who demonstrate little regard for the suffering they cause, do not necessarily possess an internal boundary preventing them from extending that exploitation to others. Why should we assume they will stop? That question sits at the forefront of my mind when I think about Donald Trump. In 1973, the same year I discovered racial discrimination in apartment rentals through my high school experiment in California, the U.S. Department of Justice sued Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump, and their real estate company for allegedly discriminating against Black apartment seekers in New York. Federal investigators documented Black applicants being told that apartments were unavailable while white applicants were offered vacancies. The case ended in a 1975 consent decree requiring changes to the company's rental practices, although the Trumps denied wrongdoing and admitted no liability. I find the historical parallel difficult to ignore. More than fifty years later, Donald Trump occupies the most powerful political office in the country. I cannot claim that the housing discrimination allegations of 1973 shed light on every decision he has made since. But I can ask why Americans should disregard that history when evaluating how he exercises power today. For me, this is not simply a question about whether someone harbors racial animus. It is a question about what we should learn when a person or institution is credibly accused of exploiting people with limited power—and what happens when that person subsequently acquires vastly greater power. The people who are easiest to exploit today are not necessarily the only people who will be vulnerable tomorrow. That is precisely why I believe Martin Luther King Jr.'s warning deserves to be understood not only as a moral principle, but as a warning about power itself. That question is at the heart of what I call my Foothold Theory . Related: Foothold Theory: How Authoritarian Power Erodes Rights by Targeting the Least Protected First Those seeking to accumulate power and wealth often find their easiest opportunities among people with the least ability to resist. These populations are the low-hanging fruit. They may be politically marginalized, economically vulnerable, or already regarded with suspicion or contempt. Existing prejudice makes their mistreatment easier to justify. The public may be persuaded that the victims deserve their circumstances, exaggerate their suffering, or pose a threat requiring extraordinary measures. Once those justifications succeed, the exploiters gain a foothold. They establish that protections can be weakened, rights disregarded, and certain people made to bear burdens others would never accept. They also discover what the public will tolerate. The immediate victims suffer, but those responsible may gain something more enduring: wealth, political influence, institutional power, or precedents that enable further exploitation. And there is no reason to assume their ambitions will remain confined to their original targets. Those people were simply the easiest place to begin. This does not mean every injustice is part of a coordinated conspiracy or that every economic decision causing harm reflects malicious intent. But we should judge powerful people and institutions by their conduct, what they gain, and whether they seek to weaken safeguards protecting others. When those entrusted with power demonstrate a willingness to exploit people who cannot effectively resist, we should not mistake the vulnerability of their first victims for a limit on their ambitions. The Danger Does Not Stay Contained Consider housing. For generations, racial exclusion enabled some Americans to accumulate property wealth while denying others similar opportunities. Today's housing affordability crisis has additional causes, including insufficient construction, restrictive land-use policies, and the growing importance of inherited wealth. But the history reveals what happens when powerful interests protect economic advantages while others are denied a basic necessity. Labor offers another example. When workers lose collective bargaining power, employers gain greater discretion over wages, benefits, and working conditions. Black workers were especially vulnerable to discrimination and industrial displacement. But weakened labor protections do not threaten only Black workers. They affect employees across racial lines. The 2007–2008 foreclosure crisis offers an especially stark illustration. Black and Latino borrowers were disproportionately exposed to predatory and high-cost mortgage lending. When the housing market collapsed, those communities suffered devastating losses. But the consequences spread throughout the national economy. The crisis had multiple causes. Nevertheless, the treatment of vulnerable borrowers revealed dangers within a financial system willing to profit from risks others would ultimately bear. The warning was there. Too many people treated it as someone else's problem. Why This Matters to Political Leadership This article is part of a larger examination of political leadership, historical knowledge, and responsibility in Los Angeles. In Part 1, I questioned what it means when someone seeking to become mayor demonstrates an inadequate appreciation of the history of Black Angelenos and their relationship with the LAPD. The issue was never simply remembering names or dates. It was understanding how institutions acquire power, how that power has been exercised, and who suffers the consequences. The disappearance of Black Los Angeles raises the same question in the economic sphere. A mayor cannot single-handedly reverse decades of racial discrimination, restore manufacturing jobs, or eliminate economic inequality. But the mayor of Los Angeles is not powerless. The mayor helps determine the city's budget priorities, appoints department leaders and commissioners, influences housing and development policies, and oversees agencies responsible for enforcing important local protections. Those responsibilities have real consequences. A mayor who understands the history of housing discrimination can strengthen the city's response to discriminatory practices and support policies that expand access to affordable housing. A mayor who appreciates the importance of labor protections can prioritize enforcement of wage laws, protect workers from retaliation, and support stronger standards for employers doing business with the city. And a mayor who recognizes how powerful interests exploit vulnerable populations can scrutinize development decisions, public contracts, and policies that transfer economic benefits to the powerful while imposing costs on those least able to bear them. None of these powers is unlimited. The City Council, state and federal governments, courts, and private economic forces all shape what a mayor can accomplish. But those limitations make sound judgment more important, not less. Historical knowledge is not an ornament of political leadership. It is a tool for recognizing danger. Without it, leaders may mistake exploitation for ordinary economic activity, discrimination for individual misfortune, and the concentration of wealth and power for inevitable progress. The question is not whether a mayor can solve every problem. It is whether the person entrusted with the city's executive authority understands these problems well enough to recognize when government is helping perpetuate them—and has the judgment and determination to use the powers of the office to challenge them. The Warning We Failed to Hear The disappearance of Black Los Angeles is not simply a story about a community losing its foothold in a city it helped build. It is a warning about what happens when economic security erodes, discrimination persists, and those benefiting from unequal arrangements accumulate still more wealth and power. What if we had recognized the struggles of Black communities as warnings about the direction of the entire society? What if we had paid attention not only to those suffering, but also to those benefiting from their vulnerability? The Miner's Canary tells us to pay attention when vulnerable populations begin to suffer. My Foothold Theory tells us to pay attention to those willing to cause or tolerate that suffering—and to the power they gain when society allows them to proceed. One identifies the warning. The other helps explain how the danger expands. Ignorance of how power gains more power, and how wealth concentrates in the hands of those willing to exploit others, endangers us all. The question is no longer simply where Black Los Angeles went. It is whether America will recognize what its disappearance was telling us before still more communities experience the same loss of economic security. And whether the people we entrust with political power understand enough about that history to prevent the pattern from continuing. Part 1 " Nithya Raman, Daryl Gates, and the History a Mayor Should Know " Part 2 “Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? History, Race, Immigration, and Political Responsibility.” Part 3 examines immigration enforcement and modern surveillance, asking whether the tools used against vulnerable populations threaten everyone's civil liberties. articles.title: Minneapolis Refused to Take Trump’s Bait. It Paid Off.
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content: All signs point toward a resounding rebuke of Donald Trump in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats have opened up a commanding lead in national polls , Trump’s popularity has sunk to historic lows, and even many of his former supporters are turning against him. There are plenty of reasons for this collapse, from rising prices to Trump’s disastrous war with Iran. But we shouldn’t forget what was arguably the single most important turning point of his presidency: the defeat of his militarized assault on Minneapolis. In January, Trump’s administration set out to terrorize immigrants, crush resistance, and establish the precedent that federal forces could occupy American cities against the wishes of their residents and elected officials. Instead, it encountered a mass movement whose courage and discipline forced Washington into a humiliating retreat. The political fallout was immediate. By late January, a Reuters poll found Trump’s overall approval had fallen to 38 percent, matching its lowest point of his second term to date. His approval on immigration, previously his strongest political asset, had sunk to 39 percent. Minneapolis had helped turn Trump’s signature political strength into a liability. In retrospect, this outcome can seem inevitable. Surely Trump’s attacks were so excessive, his agents so brutal, and the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti so shocking that a national backlash was bound to follow? But nothing was predetermined. Indeed, there’s compelling evidence that Trump and his advisers had a plan with a real chance of working: provoke Minnesota into a social explosion, whose grassroots violence and property destruction would serve as a pretext for polarizing the country and escalating Trump’s crackdown on dissent and democracy nationwide. Similar strategies have worked for authoritarian governments in other times and places. In Minneapolis, the trap failed because of the movement’s exceptionally high level of organization and nonviolent discipline. The Provocation It’s clear that ICE, under administration orders, was consciously provoking the people of Minneapolis this past winter. Thousands of heavily armed, poorly trained federal agents flooded the Twin Cities. Masked officers conducted aggressive raids, detained residents, confronted legal observers, and deployed chemical weapons against protesters. On January 7, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and killed Renée Good, a thirty-seven-year-old mother. And rather than de-escalate, Washington doubled down. On January 13, Trump warned Minnesota that a “DAY OF RECKONING & RETRIBUTION” was coming. Two days later, he threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act unless Minnesota officials stopped the supposed “professional agitators and insurrectionists” confronting ICE. Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem confirmed that military intervention had been discussed. And by January 18, the Pentagon had placed roughly 1,500 active-duty soldiers on prepare-to-deploy orders. The administration was preparing the ground for deploying the military. Nor do we have to guess how some White House officials hoped events would unfold. On January 17, Zeteo reported that two administration officials acknowledged that figures inside the White House would welcome significant violence by Minneapolis protesters. One senior official said they “would not mind it” if such violence provided a pretext for invoking the Insurrection Act. In other words, widespread disorder wouldn’t have been a setback for Trump’s strategy. It could have provided exactly the excuse he needed. The logic was straightforward: Provoke confrontations through extraordinary federal aggression. Wait for enraged protesters and community members to retaliate with widespread violence or property destruction. Then portray the movement as an anarchic threat to public safety, rally Americans around the need for order, and justify an unprecedented expansion of federal military power. Recent revelations make the administration’s methods even more disturbing. As Wired reported this week, federal investigators infiltrated activist organizations and communications networks on an extraordinary scale. Attorney Kevin Riach, representing one of fifteen Minnesota activists facing federal charges, has argued in court that undercover agents participated in organizing groups while seeking to entice participants into criminal activity. The strategy was hardly irrational. Research shows that property destruction, even on a limited scale, can sharply undermine public support for protests. It would not have taken much for Trump to transform a confrontation about federal repression into a national argument about supposedly violent leftists and blue-city disorder. Imagine the aftermath of Good’s killing had Minneapolis descended into sustained rioting, widespread vandalism, and attacks on ICE or local police. How long before the national conversation shifted away from the shooting itself toward whether Trump should restore order and whether movements should oppose property destruction and violence? Why Minneapolis Didn’t Take the Bait Trump’s central miscalculation wasn’t underestimating the anger his agents would generate. It was choosing to stage this provocation in one of the most deeply organized progressive metropolitan areas in the United States. Minnesota has a rich, decades-long tradition of labor, immigrant-rights, and religious organizing. Groups including Unidos MN, ISAIAH, Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 26, and the Twin Cities teachers’ unions had spent years developing relationships, training leaders, winning reforms, and building the capacity to act together. As SEIU Local 26 President Greg Nammacher explained , their January resistance would not have succeeded without years of preparation: “We would not have met it if we had not built a capacity beforehand.” These organizations saw clearly that a violent confrontation on Trump’s terms was one the movement was likely to lose. As JaNaé Bates Imari, co–executive director of the faith-based organization ISAIAH, explained in an interview on The Dig : Part of what is happening in Minnesota is a needling by the federal government to try to get us to respond in a particular way. And Minnesotans across the spectrum have said we will not take the bait . . . . No one [is] confused about who the peacekeepers are in the midst of what’s taking place. Crucially, organizers went beyond merely preaching restraint by building the organizational capacity to turn restraint into a collective practice. Unidos developed mass trainings for legal observation of ICE operations, ultimately training approximately thirty thousand people. ISAIAH trained hundreds of clergy, while allied groups trained thousands in nonviolent civil disobedience. Neighborhood Signal chats sprang up. Residents organized to document immigration raids, distribute whistles, support families sheltering at home, and mobilize neighbors. There were genuine pressures toward escalation. Some protesters threw objects at officers, and instances of vandalism occurred. After witnessing federal violence, not everyone agreed about the limits of confrontation. But breaking with unstrategic leftist norms about a “diversity of tactics,” the movement’s leading organizations had developed the relationships and legitimacy needed to establish collective norms about disciplined nonviolent mass action. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that protesters confronted a suspicious flag-burner and that participants in organizing chats rebuked and expelled people proposing violence. By cultivating shared expectations, training participants, challenging provocations, and giving people effective alternatives, the Minneapolis movement provided opponents of ICE with something more powerful to do than express their fury. On January 23, an estimated 75,000 or more people marched through downtown Minneapolis in subzero weather during the Day of Truth and Freedom strike action. According to organizers, roughly a thousand businesses, overwhelmingly small businesses, participated in the work stoppage. The movement’s militant resistance and discipline helped keep the attention on federal agents’ terrorization of Minneapolis’s undocumented community, as well as the heroism of two innocent Americans who decided to stand up for their neighbors. Renée Good and Alex Pretti were ordinary people who resisted injustice and paid with their lives. But their deaths alone would not necessarily have been enough to defeat the administration’s offensive. Because without an organized movement committed to preventing mass violence and property destruction, their killings could have become entangled in a debate over which side was responsible for the disorder. Instead, Trump lost control of events and the narrative. The Warning From France We don’t have to rely entirely on hypothetical scenarios to see what might have happened otherwise. France’s growing protests this fall against the cost of living and the government have recently provided a troubling counterexample. What began with high school students protesting deteriorating educational conditions in September grew into a broader movement drawing in unions, Yellow Vests, and other groups demanding economic and political change. But on October 17, huge demonstrations across the country were accompanied by extensive violence and destruction. Shops were looted in Paris, public buildings attacked, and Marseille’s city hall vandalized. Remarkably, Le Monde reported that the government had deployed only about sixty thousand police nationwide — tens of thousands fewer than normal — even though intelligence services had warned of a high risk of violence and looting. Before October 17, much of the national discussion had focused on police repression and the legitimacy of the protesters’ grievances. Afterward the government seized the opportunity to recast the confrontation as a battle against disorder. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu attacked the radical-left La France Insoumise, while politicians on the Right demanded harsher policing. The events on October 17 were a gift to the right. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen received the most positive assessments of any major political figure’s response. And an Ipsos survey found that 55 percent of French respondents believed the leftist party La France Insoumise had contributed to the tensions and violence. As historian Luca Provenzano has argued , allowing disorder to spread can itself be a highly effective state strategy. During France’s May 1968 upheaval, for example, authorities shifted from highly visible repression toward a more restrained police posture that created space for student escalation. A subsequent Interior Ministry assessment concluded that protesters’ excesses had helped restore support for order. The Right went on to win a sweeping electoral victory . Whether the French government deliberately allowed the October 2026 violence to unfold is not yet established. But the danger doesn’t depend on proving a grand conspiracy. A state can benefit from disorder whether it consciously encourages it or simply takes advantage when it erupts. That’s precisely the trap Minneapolis avoided. The Fight Ahead Of course, Trumpism is far from defeated. We don’t know exactly how badly MAGA will lose on Tuesday, and even a decisive electoral rebuke won’t automatically stop his political prosecutions, authoritarian ambitions, or continued mass deportations. Trump could still try to manipulate or reject unfavorable election results, whether next week or in 2028. He could again seek to provoke widespread disorder and use the ensuing fear to justify repression. To defeat Trumpism nationwide and to transform our country, we’ll need big, durable, welcoming organizations, new recruits beyond the ranks of existing college-educated activists, trusted leaders, and the ability to launch rapid, disciplined nonviolent action when necessary. The best way to honor Renée Good and Alex Pretti — and to thank the people of Minneapolis for their courage and sacrifice — is to learn from what they achieved. Mass nonviolent resistance doesn’t happen automatically. It has to be organized. And when it is, even the most powerful government on earth can be forced to retreat.
